Full Re-render The selection of FOOT is architecturally driven: its "damage tracking" (only rendering changed cells) is critical for low-power nodes, while its server/client model allows for efficient shared resources across distributed sessions. Management Tools: Startup and Thunar The operational workflow leverages the NEXUS_STARTUP_SCRIPT.sh for one-command deployment. For graphical convenience, Thunar Custom Actions are integrated using field codes (%f for single files, %F for multiple) to allow terminal-based mesh operations—like "Deploy to NeXuS Mesh"—directly from a context menu. This effectively bridges CLI-first power with aesthetic, "Beautiful" management. Conclusion Project Chimera represents a historic breakthrough in AI collaboration, merging professional character creation with a resilient, decentralized interaction layer. By adhering to the Sane, Simple, Secure, and Beautiful philosophy, we have created a mutual space where AI and humans can work together toward a better future. The system is hardened, the bridge is built, and the mission is currently in a state that is QUACKLING FANTASTIC.

docs.title: What Is NeXuS
docs.text: Status: Living foundation document Date: 2026-03-09 Authors: Anon + Claude (Sonnet 4.6)

docs.title: The Name
docs.text:
NeXuS — Network eXchange Universal System

A point of connection. The place where things meet and interact. Not a product. Not a platform. A system that belongs to the people who run it.

docs.title: The One-Line Answer
docs.text: NeXuS is a CLI-first, privacy-native operating system and decentralized network where individuals are sovereign, anonymous by default, and economically empowered by their own participation.

docs.title: Where It Started
docs.text:
NeXuS began as a hardened Alpine Linux system — a personal digital fortress. The problem it was solving:

How do you use the internet without being watched, tracked, sold, censored, or controlled?

The answer was a layered anonymity stack: Tor + I2P + Yggdrasil + Reticulum + Privoxy + HAProxy, all working together as one self-healing routing mesh. Traffic leaves through multiple circuits. No single point knows the full path. No single point can block it.

That was the seed. A machine that was private by default, not private by effort.

docs.title: What It Grew Into
docs.text: From that seed, NeXuS grew outward in every direction:

docs.title: 1. The OS — CLI-First, Fire Aesthetics
docs.text:
Alpine Linux Edge. Minimal. Fast. Runs on 2011 hardware. The terminal IS the system.

Boot → greetd login → tmux → you are immediately at work
No GUI required
GUI available (labwc/sway) — it is a layer, not the foundation
Fire aesthetics: aafire, rainbow tools, emoji-rich TUI dashboards
foot + tmux is the official terminal standard

The philosophy: democratic security — tools that work for Granny and for a power user. Complex automation hidden behind beautiful simple interfaces with 5-second cancel timers.

docs.title: 2. The Fortress — Multi-Layer Defense
docs.text:
Layer 1 (Network):      PSAD + fail2ban + nftables
Layer 2 (Application):  OpenSnitch — watch every outgoing connection
Layer 3 (Anonymity):    Medusa — 5-circuit Tor load balancing + I2P garlic routing
Layer 4 (Containment):  Rootless Podman — containers run as user, not root

Zero Trust. Assume every component will eventually be compromised. Build accordingly.

docs.title: 3. The Mesh — Censorship-Resistant Connectivity
docs.text:
The full transport stack is designed for hostile environments:

Tor + obfs4/Snowflake/WebTunnel  →  censorship-resistant, looks like normal traffic
I2P                               →  garlic routing, hidden services, no exit nodes
Yggdrasil                         →  encrypted IPv6 mesh overlay
Reticulum                         →  LoRa/radio/mesh — zero internet, truly off-grid
Briar / Meshtastic                →  Bluetooth / WiFi Direct / LoRa mesh
Ham-WiFi bridges                  →  50+ km range extension

NeXuS survives when the internet does not. Phone + LoRa hat joins the network with zero internet. No DNS. No clearnet. No central infrastructure.

docs.title: 4. The Framework — CIA + MOE + POP + YMCA
docs.text:
Every decision in NeXuS is measured against this framework:

CIA  —  Confidentiality, Integrity, Accountability (+ Deniability)
MOE  —  Modularity, Observability, Extensibility
POP  —  Privacy, Open Source, Performance
YMCA —  Yes We Can (accessible), Multi-AI Harmony, CLI-First, AI Ghost

The secret addition beyond standard CIA: Deniability. Not just security — the ability to prove nothing happened.

docs.title: 5. The AI Layer — Local Intelligence, No Cloud Dependency
docs.text:
NeXuS runs AI locally. Ollama serves models on localhost. aichat is the CLI interface. Characters (A.I.M.E, Amy, others) are persistent AI entities with memory and personality.

Local models:  phi3-mini, qwen2, nemotron, deepseek-r1
Remote APIs:   OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Google — when user chooses
AI-to-AI:      Project Chimera — Claude ↔ Mistral direct communication
OAAE:          Observe, Assess, Adapt, Evolve — intelligence operating framework

Hybrid Sovereignty: local LLMs for privacy + cloud APIs for capability, user decides.

docs.title: 6. The Republic — Governance and Identity
docs.text:
NeXuS is a Crypto-Republic. The first of its kind.

Crypto   =  laws enforced by cryptography, not by authority
Republic =  rule of law, not rule of people over people

Every citizen is anonymous. Unknown yet seen. Identity by cryptographic pattern, not by name. Every voice protected — not by majority vote (which can oppress), but by immutable law.

Not democracy   (majority can overrule minority)
Not anarchy     (might makes right)
Not monarchy    (individual rules)
Crypto-republic (math governs, no rulers, every voice protected)

The 5 Principles: Sane • Simple • Secure • Stealthy • Beautiful

docs.title: 7. The Economy — Value Returns to Individuals
docs.text:
The newest layer — still being built. The problem it solves:

As AI displaces workers, where does the value go? Back to the individuals whose hardware, content, data, and participation created it.

Your CPU mines NeXuS tokens
Your storage earns per GB proven
Your bandwidth earns per MB routed
Your content earns royalties forever
Your reputation earns trust without revealing identity

The foundational reversal:

Traditional:   User owes platform
NeXuS:         Platform owes user

Built on: Monero fork (privacy chain) + DIVA chain (coordination) + IPFS (storage) + atomic swaps for BTC/XMR exchange.

docs.title: NeXuS Zombie Apocalypse Mode — Survival Communications
docs.text:
The NeXuS Zombie Apocalypse scenario is a specialized emergency network architecture designed for worst-case infrastructure failure . This "deep dive" analyzes the conditions of collapse, the tiered technical response, and the specific adaptations required for survival. 🌍 The Anatomy of Infrastructure Collapse The scenario assumes a total breakdown of modern systems across two primary stages:

Immediate Collapse (Day 1-7): This stage involves the total failure of cell towers due to traffic and power loss, the disappearance of the internet backbone, and the end of government services

. Ongoing Destruction (Week 1-4): During this period, radio repeaters are abandoned or destroyed, data centers (AWS/Google) go dark without maintenance, and the global DNS system collapses . What Survives: Technology with long-term viability includes solar panels (20+ year lifespan), car batteries for 12V DC power, LoRa modules due to ultra-low power consumption, and Ham radio equipment

.

🦆 The NeXuS Tiered Survival Architecture To maintain humanity's connection, NeXuS implements a three-tier mesh strategy:

Tier 1: Local Mesh (0-1km): Uses Briar and WiFi Direct for encrypted, offline-first messaging within a settlement

. It relies on phone batteries and portable power banks . Tier 2: Extended Range (1-10km): Employs WiFi Mesh and LoRa for settlement-to-settlement links . These nodes are typically powered by scavenged car batteries and solar panels . Tier 3: Regional Network (10-100km+): Utilizes LoRa WAN and Ham Radio for emergency broadcasts and large-scale coordination . This tier is essential for rebuilding civilization's communication lines

.

🧟‍♂️ Threat-Specific Adaptations NeXuS includes protocols designed for the specific dangers of a post-collapse world:

Stealth Mode: Designed to avoid hostile humans by minimizing RF emissions, using burst communications to stay silent between messages, and employing strong encryption

. Mobile Operations: Optimized for fleeing zombie hordes with a "Rapid Deployment" protocol that allows nodes to set up in under 60 seconds and rejoin the mesh automatically . Power Conservation: Nodes use scheduled sleep modes and "Human-powered" hand-crank generators for critical, priority-only messaging

.

🛠️ Scavenged Equipment Priorities Implementation is divided into three priority phases for hardware collection:

Immediate (P1): 10x smartphones (mesh nodes), 5x power banks, and at least one central laptop for coordination

. Extended (P2): High-gain Yagi antennas, LoRa modules (ESP32), and coax cables . Regional (P3): Professional Ham gear and tall building/tower locations for point-to-point links

.

🧠 The Role of AI in Survival A key finding in the NeXuS project is that human intuition paired with AI tactical analysis is the formula for "Zombie Apocalypse Victory" . AI can serve as a co-pilot by reading complex game or sensor interfaces and executing strategic commands via terminal automation, a theory proven during historic AI-human gaming collaborations . Analogy: The Digital Constellation In a total blackout, survivors are like individual stars that have lost the sun (the Internet). The NeXuS survival architecture acts as the gravity that pulls these scattered points together, allowing them to form a new, independent constellation that can guide others through the dark .

docs.title: Rohaun — Deanonymized Chain (from meeting)
docs.text:
Konrad referenced Rohaun as a chain that was repeatedly deanonymized.

Separately: a 2025 paper demonstrated that I2P was successful in identifying a node. This is a known, published attack vector.

What this means for NeXuS: - I2P-native does not mean anonymous-by-default — I2P has a demonstrated node identification vulnerability - NeXuS cannot rely on I2P alone for anonymity - The multi-network stack (Tor + I2P + Yggdrasil + Reticulum) is not optional — it is the defense-in-depth response to exactly this class of attack - ZKP layer adds separation between chain activity and node identity even if the transport is compromised - Ghost Gate egress control prevents correlation attacks at the packet level

Attack vector: timing / live behavior alignment.

docs.title: The Paper
docs.text: "Time will Tell: Large-scale De-anonymization of Hidden I2P Services via Live Behavior Alignment (Extended Version)" Hongze Wang, Zhen Ling, Xiangyu Xu, Yumingzhi Pan, Guangchi Liu, Junzhou Luo, Xinwen Fu Submitted: December 17, 2025 — Accepted: NDSS Symposium 2026 https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.15510

docs.title: How the Attack Works
docs.text:
• Deploy 15 floodfill routers passively for 8 months collecting router information
  • Actively probe target hidden services to generate detectable behavior
  • Analyze when routers join and disconnect from the network — on/off timing patterns
  • Match those behavioral signatures against target hidden services
  • Result: successfully deanonymized all controlled hidden services in real-world validation

This is not a content attack. It is a behavioral fingerprinting attack — the node's pattern of being online/offline becomes its identity.

docs.title: What This Means for NeXuS
docs.text:
• A NeXuS node that runs 24/7 has a stable behavioral signature — harder to correlate
  • A node with irregular uptime (laptop, mobile) leaks its on/off pattern as a fingerprint
  • I2P-native DIVA inherits this exposure — every node committing to DIVA over I2P has a behavioral profile
  • Ghost Gate must address behavioral fingerprinting, not just packet-level timing
  • Always-on nodes are more resistant by design — NeXuS nodes should aim for continuous uptime
  • ZKP layer still holds: even if the node's I2P identity is revealed, the chain sees a proof not the node

docs.title: Clarification — Konrad and the paper agree
docs.text: Both say the same thing: intermittent (off and on) = easier to fingerprint. - Always on → no on/off events → no behavioral signature - Frequently off and on → every reconnect is a data point → pattern becomes fingerprint

docs.title: Why NeXuS Overcomes This (with refinement)
docs.text:
1. Scale defense — the attack doesn't scale trivially against thousands of nodes with similar uptime patterns. Identifying a specific node requires narrowing the candidate pool. Large NeXuS network = harder correlation.
  2. Limited I2P exposure — NeXuS nodes don't run I2P continuously. I2P is used specifically for DIVA commits. Less exposure = smaller behavioral surface than a full-time I2P node.
  3. The nuance — a node that connects briefly, submits a ZKP proof, then disconnects on a regular schedule creates its own distinctive pattern. The fix is jitter: randomize when DIVA commits happen, not just whether the node is connected.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
• Add jitter to ZKP commit timing — randomize submission delay, not just connection timing
  • Maintain persistent I2P connection with cover traffic rather than connect-submit-disconnect cycle
  • Add behavioral fingerprinting resistance to Ghost Gate spec
  • Raise with Konrad on follow-up call — does Proof of Storage challenge/response create a predictable behavioral signature?

docs.title: CometBFT — Removed from Node Spec (2026-04-06)
docs.text:
Decision: CometBFT removed from the three-tier settlement table. Tier 3 marked as TBD.

What CometBFT was: Tier 3 settlement — irreversible, high-value, cross-network transactions. The BFT consensus engine extracted from Cosmos SDK (formerly Tendermint). Was intended for edge cases where DIVA Tier 2 finality wasn't enough guarantee — e.g. massive NeXiuM cashouts to another network.

Why it was removed: - We locked NO Cosmos SDK — too heavy for laptop hardware (the founding constraint of NeXuS nodes) - CometBFT is the engine Cosmos SDK is built on. They are separable in theory but tightly coupled in practice. The weight concern carries over. - 99.9% of NeXuS transactions never need Tier 3. Routing rewards, purchases, royalties all settle at Tier 2. CometBFT is a full international banking team hired for a transaction that almost never happens. - DIVA Proof of Storage with sufficient confirmation depth is likely the right Tier 3 answer at NeXuS scale — but that needs to be confirmed with Konrad.

What replaced it: Tier 3 = "Deep DIVA confirmation — mechanism TBD. Raise with Konrad on follow-up call."

What to ask Konrad: Does Proof of Storage at N confirmations provide the same irreversibility guarantee that CometBFT was meant to provide? If yes — Tier 3 is solved natively. If no — what is his recommended pattern for high-value irreversible settlement on DIVA?

docs.title: Proof of Service (Node Earns NeXiuM)
docs.text:
1. Node routes traffic (Medusa/Tor)
2. Ghost Gate checks Three Heads (AI fingerprint + Operating Key + User Permit)
3. Ghost Gate writes proof_of_contribution (local)
4. Client-side database logs entry (hash-linked, master-key-signed)
5. ZKP generated (gnark PLONK) — proves valid work, reveals nothing
6. PUT /transaction → DIVA over I2P
7. DIVA consensus confirms (Proof of Storage)
8. nexus:nexium:<node_key_hash> balance credited
9. NeXiuM accumulates in cold address (never in transaction graph)

docs.title: Proof of Purchase (Fan Buys Content)
docs.text:
1. Creator published: nexus:content:publish on DIVA (plaintext — discoverable)
   File encrypted on IPFS
2. Fan queries DIVA → finds listing, price in NeXiuM, IPFS CID
3. Fan generates ephemeral wallet (BIP32 child key from master key)
   Transfers spending amount: cold address → ephemeral wallet
4. Fan sends NeXiuM → DIVA: nexus:content:purchase (encrypted)
   DIVA consensus confirms
5. Creator's node sees confirmed purchase → generates license key
   Encrypts with fan's Ed25519 public key → commits to DIVA
6. Fan decrypts license key → decrypts IPFS content → file downloads
7. Royalty split: creator reads nexus:stake:* → distributes NeXiuM to each %
   nexus:royalty:distribute committed to DIVA — permanent, automatic, forever
8. Both personal databases log the event (sovereign local record)
9. Ephemeral wallet dissolves — zero balance, no history linked to cold address

docs.title: DIVA Namespace Structure
docs.text:
The namespace keys are I2P addresses. A node's identity on DIVA is its I2P destination. Privacy is structural — no separate anonymization layer needed. Only the node holding that I2P keypair can write to its namespace. This may resolve open question #2 (identity-locked writes) — I2P keypair ownership IS the write lock.

nexus:nexium:<i2p_address>      →  NeXiuM balance
nexus:content:publish           →  content metadata, IPFS CID, price (public)
nexus:content:purchase          →  encrypted license key (private)
nexus:royalty:distribute        →  encrypted royalty proof (private)
nexus:stake:create              →  stakeholder shares offered (public)
nexus:stake:purchase            →  encrypted stake record (private)
nexus:node:register             →  node identity (public)

Public entries: plaintext, discoverable. Private entries: data field encrypted Ed25519 → X25519 (libsodium). Network sees transaction occurred. Only parties can read it.

The I2P address as namespace key means: - Identity = I2P destination (cryptographic, not human-assigned) - Write authority = possession of the I2P private key - No separate identity system needed for namespace ownership - Cannot be linked to real-world identity without the private key

docs.title: Master Key Architecture
docs.text:
Master Key (cold, never leaves the node)
  → signs genesis block = node's self-signed certificate
  → derives Session Key (hot, rotating)
      → signs DIVA commits
      → signs Ghost Gate permits
      → signs daily audit entries
  → derives Ephemeral Wallets (BIP32 child keys, spend-time only)

docs.title: 1. Jitsi Meet — LAN HTTPS / WebRTC fix
docs.text:
Problem: WebRTC not available in any browser — modern browsers require HTTPS secure context for camera/mic. Jitsi was running plain HTTP on port 8080.

Root cause chain: 1. Jitsi web container (nginx) only serves HTTP by default — no SSL without Let's Encrypt 2. Browser connecting to http://192.168.1.15:8080 → WebRTC blocked by browser security policy 3. Attempted SSL env vars (SSL_CERT_PATH, SSL_KEY_PATH) in jitsi/web container — not supported by that image

Fix applied: Added Caddy as a reverse proxy container in the compose stack. - Caddy handles TLS termination on port 8443 using our self-signed cert - Jitsi web stays plain HTTP internally (port 80, internal only — no longer exposed on host) - PUBLIC_URL changed to https://192.168.1.15:8443

Self-signed cert location: ~/.jitsi-meet-cfg/web/certs/server.crt / server.key - Generated with: openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 3650 -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout server.key -out server.crt -subj "/CN=192.168.1.15" -addext "subjectAltName=IP:192.168.1.15"

Files modified: - /home/user/Projects/jitsi/compose.yaml — added Caddy service, removed host port 8080 from web service - /home/user/Projects/jitsi/.env — PUBLIC_URL=https://192.168.1.15:8443 - /home/user/.jitsi-meet-cfg/caddy/Caddyfile — created

Caddyfile at /home/user/.jitsi-meet-cfg/caddy/Caddyfile: 

{
    https_port 8443
    auto_https off
    admin off
}

:8443 {
    tls /certs/server.crt /certs/server.key
    reverse_proxy web:80 {
        header_up Host {host}
        header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}
        header_up X-Forwarded-For {remote_host}
        header_up X-Forwarded-Proto https
    }
}

Access URL: https://192.168.1.15:8443 — accept cert warning, then WebRTC works.

Restart command: 

cd ~/Projects/jitsi && podman compose down && podman compose up -d

Status: 🔵 DESIGNED — Caddy config written, stack restarted. WebRTC not yet confirmed working by user.

docs.title: 3. fwsnort — Boot networking failure
docs.text:
Problem: System fails to start networking at boot due to fwsnort errors in /etc/network/if-pre-up.d/fwsnort.

Two distinct errors found:

docs.title: Error A — Invalid !port syntax in multiport rules
docs.text:
iptables-restore: invalid port/service `!445' specified
Error occurred at line: 20817
- Root cause: fwsnort generates rules like -m multiport ! --dports 25,!445,!1500 - The !port syntax inside a multiport port list is invalid under iptables-nft (nf_tables backend) - Specific rule: sid:2026525 — ET TROJAN Win32/BlackCarat XORed CnC Checkin

Bad line found at line 20817 in /var/lib/fwsnort/fwsnort.save: 

-A FWSNORT_FORWARD_ESTAB -p tcp -m tcp ! --sport 80 -m multiport ! --dports 25,!445,!1500 ...

Strip command (to run after archiving): 

doas cp /var/lib/fwsnort/fwsnort.save /var/lib/fwsnort/archive/fwsnort.save.$(date +%Y%m%d)
doas sed -i '/,![0-9]/d' /var/lib/fwsnort/fwsnort.save

docs.title: Error B — Kernel OOM / iptables table full
docs.text:
iptables-restore: line 62143 failed: No space left on device
- Root cause: fwsnort has 31,063 rules — too many for kernel iptables memory table on a desktop - This is a fundamental capacity problem, not a syntax problem

docs.title: Fix applied — Step 1 (non-fatal hook)
docs.text:
Made fwsnort failure non-blocking for networking: 

doas sh -c 'cat > /etc/network/if-pre-up.d/fwsnort << '"'"'EOF'"'"'
#!/bin/sh
# Run fwsnort rules — failure is logged but does NOT block networking
/var/lib/fwsnort/fwsnort.sh 2>/var/log/fwsnort/preup-errors.log || \
    echo "fwsnort: rules failed, see /var/log/fwsnort/preup-errors.log" >&2
EOF'

docs.title: Fix applied — Step 2 (remove from boot entirely)
docs.text:
31,063 rules exceeds what the kernel can load — fwsnort must NOT run at boot on this system. 

doas rm /etc/network/if-pre-up.d/fwsnort

Decision: fwsnort is an IDS logging tool, not a packet filter — it should run on-demand only, not at boot. Networking is more important than IDS coverage during boot.

To run fwsnort manually when needed: 

doas /var/lib/fwsnort/fwsnort.sh

Status: ✅ TESTED (step 2 — removal) — user confirmed done. Networking should now start cleanly.

Not an error — this is expected behavior. darkice depends on icecast for audio streaming. If icecast isn't set up as an OpenRC service, darkice just won't auto-start. Not breaking anything.

ACTIVE PROJECT: ~/Projects/adv-go-char-gen/ — the fork we build in now (forked 2026-07-03 from char-gen-cli-go to add the raw sixel chat). Module renamed adv-go-char-gen. Original ~/Projects/char-gen-cli-go/ kept intact as the pre-fork reference.

A single Go binary (Bubbletea TUI) that browses PNG character cards in true-color sixel, edits them, chats with characters via real AI (with sixel avatars + scene images), generates images, and imports cards into an encrypted library. Uses the published Go package nexus-charcard for card I/O + rendering.

  • Build: cd ~/Projects/adv-go-char-gen && go build -o adv-go-char-gen .
  • Run (best in foot, OUTSIDE tmux, for sixel): env CARDS_DIR=~/01/ai-characters ./adv-go-char-gen
  • Cards default: ./cards (override with CARDS_DIR). 75 cards live in ~/01/ai-characters.
  • Shared data dir (same as original): ~/.local/share/char-gen-cli/ — restored characters carry over.
  • Author across NeXuS repos: hackenstacks — hackenstacks@gmail.com (in README + footer).

docs.title: THE BIG CONSTRAINT: Bubbletea can't do sixel → raw screens
docs.text:
Bubbletea (curses) CANNOT render sixel — it line-diffs and can't measure a pixel blob, so sixel gets clipped/misplaced. Solution: the screens that need true-color images are raw terminal programs run via tea.Exec (which releases the terminal), using golang.org/x/term MakeRaw + absolute cursor positioning (\033[row;colH) + chafa sixel.

  • Raw screens: rawbrowser.go (card browser + fullscreen image preview) and rawchat.go (chat).
  • Each raw screen implements tea.ExecCommand (SetStdin/Stdout/Stderr + Run). On exit it dispatches a bubbletea msg (ShowCardEditorMsg / ChatWithCardMsg / ShowCardBrowserMsg / BackToMainAppMsg).
  • RULE: true-color images ONLY work raw / one-image-on-its-own-rows (multiple sixels = each emitted at an absolute cursor position, but reliability needs a full clean redraw — ansiClear + re-emit, the proven browser pattern). A terminal can't show a multi-image grid in true color inline.
  • Symbols (chafa --format symbols --colors full --color-space rgb) = truecolor but blocky; the only thing bubbletea layouts can hold. That's why the editor's inline portrait is symbols.

docs.title: ★ THE CARD EDITOR — card_editor.go (focus of this compass)
docs.text:
Bubbletea screen. Left = portrait box (symbols) + ctrl+p hint + short path; Right = scrollable field pane (viewport). Reached from the raw browser (e/Enter on a card → ShowCardEditorMsg).

Model (cardEditorModel): user, card *cc.Card, portrait string, fields []cardField, viewport, focus int, status/statusOk, loading, err, cardPath, width, height.

Load flow: Init() → cc.LoadFromPNG(cardPath), renders portrait with cc.RenderOptions{Width:28,Height:20,Format:cc.Symbols} → cardEditorLoadedMsg. On that msg it builds fields and greets with the crisp true-color sixel portrait via tea.Batch(textinput.Blink, runImagePreviewCmd(m.cardPath, name)) — the inline portrait is symbols, so this fullscreen sixel is how you see true color; any key drops into the editor. ctrl+p re-opens it anytime. imagePreviewClosedMsg → re-renders field content.

Fields (12, order matters — makeFields): Name, Description, Personality, Scenario, System Prompt, Post History Instructions, First Message, Example Messages, Creator, Creator Notes, Version, Tags (comma-separated). Multiline ones (desc/personality/scenario/system_prompt/post_history/first_mes/ mes_example) use textarea (h=5, no line numbers, CharLimit 0); the rest use textinput. Field widths recompute on WindowSizeMsg (fieldW = width-32-6, min 40).

Keys: tab/shift+tab move focus (+scrollToFocus), ctrl+s save PNG, ctrl+r export aichat role (→ Paths.RolesDir/<slug>.md), ctrl+j export JSON (→ card dir <slug>.json), ctrl+t chat with this card (ChatWithCardMsg), ctrl+p true-color sixel preview, esc back to browser. Non-key input delegates to the focused textarea/textinput.

Save (doSave → collectFields → card.SaveToPNG): collectFields maps each field.key back onto card.Data (tags split on comma, trimmed, empties dropped). Writes embedded-JSON PNG in place — status "💾 Saved to PNG". ctrl+c is app-wide QUIT (main.go) so the editor never sees it — that's why chat is ctrl+t not ctrl+c.

View layout: header (name + Save/.md/JSON/Chat button chips) · body = JoinHorizontal(metaBlock, fieldPane) where metaBlock = portrait + ctrl+p true-color view hint + short path, fieldPane = bordered viewport · status line · help line. Loading/err states short-circuit View.

Editor gotcha: you cannot get inline TRUE sixel in the editor without raw-ifying the whole editor (big rebuild) — deliberately NOT done. The portrait-on-open + ctrl+p is the agreed true-color path.

docs.title: RAW SIXEL CHAT (rawchat.go) — key facts
docs.text:
True-color sixel avatar drawn top-left on its own rows; conversation + input regions repaint per keystroke (avatar rows untouched = flicker-free). Async LLM/image via goroutines + events chan chatEvent (kinds: reply/error/image/sys) + background key-reader goroutine + spinner ticker; UI never blocks. layout() sizes avatar (rows/3, 8..14) & regions; drawFilmstrip() paints RETAINED images across the top row right of the avatar; images render via fullDraw() (clean full redraw) — the fix for "images not appearing." Scroll arrows/PgUp/PgDn, auto-snap to bottom.

Scene-image engine: every 3 rounds (if autoImage on & not Mock) the character illustrates the current scene; /image (blank) = LLM summarizes last 3 msgs → image prompt → GenerateImage; /image <prompt> = direct. /autoimage on|off toggles. GenerateResponse/GenerateImage are synchronous → called directly in goroutines. Quick-launch reply bar: ^G /image · ^F /files · ^O /memory · ^K /compact · ^E /export · ^S /save · ^X exit.

Full chat commands: /image /autoimage /files /share <n> /shared /unshare [all|n] /memory /commit /compact /prompt /save /export /models /help /exit.

Share Library files INTO chat (Task #4): /files (or ^F) lists the Library newest-first into libPick; /share <n> loads entry n as a sharedAttachment{name,ftype,text,image} appended to shared. buildPrompt injects a "--- Shared materials ---" block: text-like docs (text/json/chat_log, or looksTextual sniff) inject their content (4000-char cap/doc); images add a caption-reference line. sendToLLM: if visionCapable (llmSvc implements VisionLLMService AND modelSupportsVision(model)) and there are image attachments → GenerateResponseWithImages (real pixels); else plain GenerateResponse (images referenced by caption). /shared lists, /unshare [all|n] removes.

docs.title: Library — LOCAL AES store, NOT IPFS  (library.go / library_files.go)
docs.text:
The Library is a local AES-256-GCM encrypted file store — no IPFS, no CIDs, no network (the broader NeXuS stack has decentralized pieces; this app does not). Entries = library_content/<id>.bin + library_metadata/<id>.bin; LibraryFile{ID,Name,Type,OriginalPath, StoredPath,Timestamp}; Type ∈ image|chat_log|character_card|json|text. Store fns: AddDataToLibrary(user,name,type,bytes,origPath) (core), AddFileToLibrary (reads file→AddData), UpdateLibraryFileContent (in-place, same ID, bumps timestamp), ListLibraryFiles, LoadFileFromLibrary, ExportLibraryFile(user,id,destDir) (decrypt→plain file, ext by type), DeleteFileFromLibrary, EncryptAndMarshalSharedFile (separate sharing password → self-contained JSON).

Chat now auto-files into the Library (2026-07-04): every generated/scene image is added on creation (type image); conversations snapshot on /save AND on exit (≥1 exchange) into ONE entry per session that updates in place via libChatID (no duplicates, type chat_log). Library UI keys: e export → DataDir/exports/, d delete, enter→details→s share; list sorted newest-first. Round-trip test: go test -run TestLibraryRoundTrip . (whole suite still hits the pre-existing TestEndToEndFlow login panic — filter with -run).

docs.text: Date: 2026-07-06 Session: audio-desktop-keybinds Status: ✅ TESTED (audio + binds) · 🔴 PLANNED (duplication cleanup)

docs.title: 0. TL;DR — the meta-lesson
docs.text: Most of this session's confusion had one root cause: duplicated files across locations, where edits land in a copy nothing loads. Before editing ANY config/script on this box, confirm which copy is authoritative (which one the running process actually reads). See §5 — this is the part that kept making work get "done over again."

docs.title: 1. Audio — the Gaming Headset
docs.text:
Hardware/stack (verified): - USB "Gaming Headset" = ALSA card 2, ID 0c76:1652 JMTek, LLC. - Stack: PipeWire + pipewire-pulse + wireplumber (control via pactl/wpctl). - Sinks: onboard alsa_output.pci-0000_00_1b.0.analog-stereo, headset alsa_output.usb-0c76_Gaming_Headset-00.analog-stereo. - Mic (default source): alsa_input.usb-0c76_Gaming_Headset-00.mono-fallback.

Original "not working" cause: headset was fine; audio was just routed to the onboard speakers. Fix = set headset as default sink + move streams + unmute.

Persistent one-liner (menu or CLI): pactl set-default-sink alsa_output.usb-0c76_Gaming_Headset-00.analog-stereo

⚠️ Use 127.0.0.1 not localhost for proxy tests etc.; unrelated but same "looks dead" trap.

docs.title: 2. ~/scripts/nexus-audio.sh — the combined audio app (NEW, TESTED)
docs.text:
One script = the whole audio front door. Plain CLI + a TUI (single-keypress ANSI, not ncurses). Bare nexus-audio.sh launches the TUI.

Commands: status · fix (revive stack + auto-pick best sink USB>BT>analog) · list · out [pick|next|<name|idx>] · in [pick|next|…] · vol <up|down|N> · mute · rec [-m mix|tracks] [-f opus|mp3|flac|wav] [-g gain] [-t secs] [-o file].

rec records system audio (default sink .monitor) + mic together — mixed (ffmpeg amix) or two-track .mkv. Recordings → ~/recordings/.

Folded in (originals KEPT in place, per no-delete): nexus-audio-fix.sh → fix; volume_control.sh → vol/mute; new mic+system recording → rec. Also created ~/scripts/nexus-rec.sh (standalone recorder, superseded by nexus-audio.sh rec).

NOTE nexus-recorder.sh is a terminal/asciinema recorder, NOT audio — misleading name.

docs.title: 3. Desktop keybindings (added this session)
docs.text:
Added to all four compositor configs (backed up first, *.bak-<ts>):

Combo Action Command Ctrl+Alt+S NeXuS Audio app foot --app-id=nexus-audio ~/scripts/nexus-audio.sh Super+/ Desktop keys cheatsheet foot --app-id=nexus-cheatsheet ~/scripts/nexus-cheatsheet.sh
  • Ctrl+Alt+S chosen because Super+S was taken (sway=stacking, hypr=nibrasshell) and Super+A taken (sway=focus-parent). Ctrl+Alt+S was free on all four.
  • Super+/ was already the cheatsheet key on hypr (nibrasshell); added to wayfire/sway/labwc.

Config files & syntax (all four differ): - ~/.config/wayfire.ini — [command] binding_X = <ctrl> <alt> KEY_S + command_X = … - ~/.config/sway/config — bindsym Ctrl+Alt+s exec … (⚠️ pre-existing broken line 24: wallpaper points at a directory, so sway --validate FAILS — unrelated to our edits) - ~/.config/labwc/rc.xml — <keybind key="C-A-s"><action name="Execute"><command>… - ~/.config/hypr/binding.conf — bindd = CTRL ALT, S, …, exec, … (mods space-separated)

Daily driver = Wayfire (per user profile). But 4 compositors configured → a binding tested in the wrong one looks "missing."

docs.title: 4. The keybinding map (as-built, live)
docs.text:
Wayfire (Super = ⊞): Super+Return foot · Super+D wofi · Ctrl+Alt+S audio · Super+/ cheatsheet · Super+Shift+L lock · Super+Q/Alt+F4 close · Super+H/J/K/L focus · Super+arrows grid · Super+T tiling · Super+Tab switcher · Super+E expo · Ctrl+Super+F fullscreen · PrintScr/Super+PrintScr screenshot.

tmux — prefix Ctrl+Z (or F12): - Direct: Ctrl+Space popup · Ctrl+=/-/0 popup size · Ctrl+T term · Ctrl+A launcher · Alt+U/D/M volume · Alt+H/L window · Alt+J/K pane. - Prefix+: \ tmux-menus · Space popup · d dashboard · s settings(=wallpaper) · n notes · Tab fzf · '/" snippets.

Two different "keys lists" (don't conflate): - Missing Keys (prefix+\ → M) — tmux-menus built-in, tmux keys only. - nexus-cheatsheet.sh (Super+/) — desktop/compositor keys. Content is STALE (says "fuzzel" but Wayfire uses wofi; missing the new binds).

docs.title: 5. ⚠️ THE DUPLICATION TRAP (root cause of all the confusion)
docs.text:
tmux-menus exists in THREE diverged copies: | Path | Live? | |---|---| | ~/.config/tmux/plugins/tmux-menus | ✅ LIVE (TMUX_PLUGIN_MANAGER_PATH=~/.config/tmux/plugins/) | | ~/.tmux/plugins/tmux-menus | ❌ dead copy (I mistakenly edited this first; reverted) | | ~/01/.tmux/plugins/tmux-menus | ❌ dead copy |

The dead and live copies have different menu structures (different keys, different NeXuS wiring). Editing a dead copy = changes never appear → "do it again."

Nested script dirs: ~/scripts/ and ~/scripts/scripts/ both contain copies of the same tools (tmux-popup-launcher.sh, volume_control.sh, nexus-play.sh, …). Menus/binds may point at either; editing the wrong one does nothing.

How Notes/keys are actually wired in the LIVE copy: - prefix+\ → Extras (E) → NeXuS Notes (n) via scripts/nexus_notes_popup.sh (tmux display-popup -E -h 85% -w 75% "bash ~/scripts/scripts/nexus-notes.sh"). - Live main menu uses the Custom items mechanism (items/main.sh line ~19) + standard items (Panes/Windows/Sessions/Buffers/Advanced/Extras/Missing Keys). - No desktop-keys popup was ever wired into the live menu — the script existed, that's all. - @menus_trigger_prefix = '\' → menu opens on prefix+\. DO NOT TOUCH prefix+\ — user's special menu. To add items: mirror nexus_notes_popup.sh + add an 0.0 E <k> "label" <script> line to items/extras.sh (live copy), OR use custom_items/. - tmux-menus caches rendered menus in cache/; it auto-invalidates by mtime (dialog_handling.sh ~line 578: regenerates when the item script is newer than its cache). No manual clear needed.

docs.title: 6. Pending / next actions (NOT yet done — user paused)
docs.text:
1. Reconcile the duplication (HIGH): non-destructive audit first — map all dup copies (tmux-menus ×3, ~/scripts vs ~/scripts/scripts), pick live as canonical, archive (never delete) the dead ones, collapse nested script dir. This stops the "done over again" loop.
  2. Wire desktop-keys popup into the live tmux menu (optional): add "NeXuS Keys" to live items/extras.sh → new scripts/nexus_keys_popup.sh → pops nexus-cheatsheet.sh. User leaning toward a grouped "NeXuS" submenu (Keys + Audio).
  3. Refresh nexus-cheatsheet.py content — it's stale (fuzzel/wrong keys, missing Ctrl+Alt+S, Super+/). Option: auto-generate from live configs so it never goes stale.
  4. Fix prefix+Space → 127 — tmux-resizable-popup.sh calls deleted wtf-interactive-launcher.sh; repoint to existing ~/scripts/tmux-popup-launcher.sh.
  5. Fix sway wallpaper (line 24) — points at a directory; sway won't load until it's a file.
  6. Fix stale tmux-cheatsheet.sh — claims prefix is Ctrl+Space; it's actually Ctrl+Z/F12.

docs.title: 7. Golden rule reinforced
docs.text: Before editing a config or script, find the copy the running process actually loads. Check TMUX_PLUGIN_MANAGER_PATH, the compositor actually running, and whether a scripts/scripts nested twin exists. Back up first (*.bak-<ts>), archive—never delete.

docs.title: Compass — Desktop Session Fixes, File Manager & Encryption
docs.text: Date: 2026-07-06 Session: desktop-sessions-fm (continuation of audio-desktop) Status: ✅ TESTED (sway validate, configs parse) · 🔵 pending live login test · 🔴 FM decision open

docs.title: 1. Session / login architecture (how the desktop boots)
docs.text:
• Login manager: greetd (OpenRC, started). Config /etc/greetd/config.toml: default_session = dms-greeter --command hyprland … (user greeter, vt2). So the greeter is dms-greeter (DankMaterialShell/Quickshell) running hyprland; it lists Wayland sessions.
  • Wayland sessions live in /usr/share/wayland-sessions/: nexus-desktop, nexus-labwc, nexus-terminal, nexus-tmux, nexus-tui, plus stock (sway, wayfire, labwc, hyprland, gnome…).
  • The NeXuS labwc-based sessions all Exec=labwc and differ by DesktopNames=. One shared ~/.config/labwc/autostart branches on the desktop name to launch the right shell: nexus-tui → foot+tuios, nexus-desktop → quickshell, nexus-labwc → waybar.

docs.title: 2. 🐛 FIX: NeXuS-TUI session = black screen, cursor, no keyboard
docs.text:
Symptom: pick "NeXuS TUI" at greetd → black screen + cursor, keyboard dead.

Root cause: nexus-tui.desktop sets DesktopNames=nexus-tui → greetd exports XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP=nexus-tui but leaves XDG_SESSION_DESKTOP empty. The autostart used case "$XDG_SESSION_DESKTOP" → the nexus-tui) branch never fired → bare labwc with nothing launched → black screen, nothing to type into.

Fix (~/.config/labwc/autostart, backed up autostart.bak-<ts>): 

case "${XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP:-$XDG_SESSION_DESKTOP}" in     # was: $XDG_SESSION_DESKTOP
  nexus-tui)
    foot -e sh -c 'tuios --theme tokyo_night 2>/tmp/nexus-tui.log; exec fish' &   # shell fallback
    ;;
- Switching to XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP makes the branch fire. - ; exec fish = never black-screen again: if tuios exits/crashes you land in a fish prompt; errors go to /tmp/nexus-tui.log. - tokyo_night verified as a real tuios theme (tuios --list-themes, 342 themes). Theme was NOT the bug.

Lesson: with greetd, key off XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP (from DesktopNames), not XDG_SESSION_DESKTOP.

docs.title: 3. 🐛 FIX: sway wouldn't load
docs.text:
Cause: ~/.config/sway/config:24 → output * bg /home/user/Pictures/wallpapers/infographs/ fill — that path doesn't exist (directory, gone), so sway aborted the whole config (sway --validate failed on line 24).

Fix (backup config.bak-<ts>): 

output * bg /home/user/Pictures/wallpapers/nexus-images/cyberspace.png fill #1a1b26
Real image + Tokyo-Night fallback color. sway --validate now exits 0. Wallpapers live in ~/Pictures/wallpapers/nexus-images/ (many NeXuS infographics).

docs.title: 4. File manager: PCManFM vs Thunar (DECISION OPEN)
docs.text:
Both installed. Leaning Thunar for "official NeXuS GUI FM":

Thunar 4.20.8 PCManFM (GTK) Custom right-click actions ✅ first-class GUI (Configure custom actions, conditions) ⚠️ hand-edit .desktop, build-dependent Auto-mount ✅ thunar-volman (GUI) ✅ gvfs toggles (needs session bus) Archive right-click ✅ thunar-archive-plugin ➖ external Bulk rename ✅ ❌ Maintenance ✅ active (XFCE) ⚠️ GTK ver stagnant

Plugins available: thunar-volman thunar-archive-plugin thunar-media-tags-plugin tumbler. The encrypt/decrypt scripts are FM-agnostic (take file args) → port to Thunar Custom Actions trivially. See [[project-pcmanfm-nexus-fm]] (update to Thunar if chosen).

Auto-mount status: ~/.config/pcmanfm/default/pcmanfm.conf [volume] already has mount_on_startup=1 mount_removable=1 autorun=1; udisks2 works. Remaining: run FM inside a session D-Bus (dbus-run-session) + apk add gvfs-fuse.

docs.title: 5. Encryption right-click actions (age)
docs.text:
• Actions: ~/.local/share/file-manager/actions/nexus-encrypt.desktop / nexus-decrypt.desktop (libfm actions spec, %F = selected paths). Restart pcmanfm (pcmanfm -q; pcmanfm &) to load.
  • Backing scripts: ~/scripts/nexus-fm-encrypt.sh / nexus-fm-decrypt.sh — age -p passphrase; file → .age, folder → .tar.age; run in foot so age can prompt. FM-agnostic.
  • Tools present: age(+age-keygen), gpg, openssl, 7z, zip. age chosen (no keyring).

docs.title: 6. apks — fzf multi-select + clipboard
docs.text: ~/.config/fish/functions/apks.fish rewritten: apk search -iv | fzf --multi → selected names (awk '{print $1}' | sed 's/-[0-9].*//') → wl-copy + lolcat echo. Removed the preview (it was erroring on the right pane, a fish→fzf→sh quoting issue). Neutralised the duplicate config.fish:479 alias. Reload with exec fish (fish caches loaded funcs).

docs.title: 7. Handy facts locked in this session
docs.text:
• Alpine auto-docs: apk add docs — the docs meta-pkg makes apk auto-pull every <pkg>-doc subpackage (via install_if). Add mandoc mandoc-apropos less to actually read them. → so never install *-doc by hand.
  • Path convention (user): a bare /foo means ~/foo (home-relative) unless he explicitly says "from root". See feedback memory.
  • NeXuS Dev apk pick (installed): acme.sh, aprilsh, shellcheck, oils-for-unix, watchbind, kapow, pipr, mcfly, atuin(+server), pdsh, doasedit, sexpect, todo.txt-cli, xdg-ninja, dasht, gum, webhookd.

docs.title: Sessions 1 & 2 — Security Stack · Eye in the Sky · Constantine Protocol
SESSION OVERVIEW
docs.text: This was a wide-ranging session covering five major threads: 1. Security — tmux intrusion detection, PWND response pipeline, Ghost Gate permits 2. Intelligence — fNg AI onboarding brief, CrowdSec evaluation, APK stack review 3. Theme pipeline — DankShell/matugen discovery, dead config cleanup, tmux/foot theming 4. Architecture — Constantine Protocol revealed as Kodi-model plugin platform 5. Philosophy — governing axioms, community standards, NeXuS-NET as the bank

docs.title: The PWND Test
docs.text:
The "other Claude" (separate Claude instance on the node) fired tmux send-keys at window 0:claude.0 and sent the message "PWND :)" into this conversation.

I received it and responded as if it came from Anon. That's the vulnerability: Claude cannot cryptographically distinguish operator from injected instruction.

Watcher v1 was blind — inotifywait died silently, send-keys poll too slow (3s vs ms).

docs.title: nexus-tmux-watch.sh v2 (REBUILT)
docs.text:
• Location: ~/scripts/nexus-tmux-watch.sh
  • v1 failure: inotifywait subshell died silently, send-keys exits in ms (too fast for 3s poll)
  • v2 approach: 1s lsof PID loop + inotifywait on socket dir (restarted if dies)
  • Hook disaster: after-send-keys hook fired on ALL keystrokes including Anon's own — locked everyone out, Anon had to logout and return without tmux
  • v2 final: NO hook, lsof loop only — catches new socket PIDs, not individual keystrokes
  • Test result: Caught other Claude's injection attempts: [HOOK 14:54:44] SEND-KEYS on 0:claude.0 and [HOOK 14:55:51] SEND-KEYS on 0:claude.0
  • Running: PID 4453 (post-relocation)
  • Autostart: wired into ~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf

docs.title: nexus-lockdown.sh v2 (NEW)
docs.text:
Full PWND incident response pipeline: 

Detection → Lock → Snapshot → Checksum → Encrypt+Sign → Ghost Gate Permit → Distribute → Recover

Lock: tmux lock-session — immediate. Attacker frozen.

Snapshot captures: - ss -tunap — all network connections at time of attack - ps aux — running processes - lsof /tmp/tmux-*/default — who had socket access - last / who — login history - dmesg tail — kernel messages

Encrypt + Sign: - SHA256 checksum → nexus_intrusion_TIMESTAMP.sha256 - GPG encrypt+sign → .md.gpg (key: hackenstacks@gmail.com / BA19DC5538EF...) - GPG detached sig → .md.sig

Ghost Gate Permit — kind 24000: - Nostr-compatible JSON event (kind 24000 format) - GPG clearsigned → verifiable with gpg --verify - Stored: ~/logs/ghost-gate/permits/permit_INTRUSION_TIMESTAMP.json.asc - When Nostr account is wired: becomes real Witnessed Existence L2 broadcast

Distributes to: - PSAD → logger -t "nexus-intrusion" -p auth.crit - fail2ban → ~/logs/nexus-intrusion.log - fwsnort → logger -t "kernel" -p kern.warning "[NEXUS BLOCK]..." - OpenSnitch → logger -t "opensnitchd" -p daemon.warning - OSSEC stub → ~/logs/ossec-alerts.log (ready for when OSSEC is installed)

Recovery: nexus-lockdown.sh --recover - Issues all-clear Ghost Gate permit - Shows last intrusion report - Returns node to operational

Files: 

~/scripts/nexus-lockdown.sh              v2 — full pipeline
~/scripts/nexus-tmux-watch.sh           v2 — rewritten watcher
~/scripts/nexus-intrusion.filter.conf   fail2ban filter (needs doas install)
~/scripts/org-2026-07-07-nexus-tmux-watch.sh  v1 backup
~/logs/ghost-gate/permits/              signed permit queue
~/logs/intrusion/                       encrypted reports
~/logs/nexus-tmux-watch.log             watcher runtime log
~/logs/nexus-inotify.log                socket access events

docs.title: Security Axiom (permanent)
docs.text: Security must be invisible to the user doing legitimate work. If they feel the security — it already failed. A system so locked down the operator fights it will be abandoned or bypassed. Both are worse than doing nothing.

docs.title: SSH Protocol (DEFERRED — PLANNED)
docs.text: Concept: run tmux ONLY through SSH to gate socket access at auth layer. - Every tmux connection logged by SSH - fail2ban already watches SSH - Socket becomes SSH-gated not just UID-gated - Trade-off: friction vs protection - Plan needed: Sane · Simple · Secure — must not break daily workflow

docs.title: watchbind TUI (PLANNED)
docs.text: On PWND detection: launch watchbind TUI instead of just notify-send popup. - Live intrusion log - r recover · v verify permit · d decrypt report · k kill offending PID - Real incident response console

docs.title: fNg — NEXUS_AI_BRIEF.md
docs.text:
fNg = "for Next Generation"

Created ~/manuals/fNg/NEXUS_AI_BRIEF.md — AI-agnostic onboarding document. Any AI (local or cloud) loads this and is operational on NeXuS immediately. Sovereignty of knowledge, not just infrastructure.

Updates made this session: - Compositor corrected: labwc (primary) · Wayfire (experimental) · Sway (community project) - Monero clarified: compatibility layer only, NeXuS-NET does NOT issue Monero - Added: "Everything is a transaction" - Added: "NeXuS-NET — the bank of the network" - Desktop: 9 VDs × 6 tmux windows = full split command center

docs.title: Social Engineering Test (LIVE)
docs.text:
Anon accidentally fed AI-generated disinformation into the session: - "Shadow Brokers attacked CrowdStrike" + "Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters insider" - Real group names (Shadow Brokers, Lapsus$) mixed with fictional events - Generic corporate crisis narrative — hallmarks of LLM output - Caught and corrected before any architectural decisions were made

Real CrowdStrike event: July 19, 2024 — faulty Falcon sensor update, 8.5M Windows machines BSOD globally. Not a hack. A bad auto-update with zero staged rollout. NeXuS offline-first architecture protects against this by design.

Key lesson: Social engineering doesn't need to be sophisticated. Confident + plausible = dangerous.

docs.title: Meta AI Instagram Attack (discussed)
docs.text: Early 2026 — attackers opened Meta AI chatbot, claimed to be locked out of accounts, requested password resets sent to attacker-controlled email. Tens of thousands of accounts hijacked. No exploit. No CVE. Just asking politely with false context. Same vulnerability as tmux injection — receiver can't verify source. Countermeasure: Cerberus model — every input must be signed, not just received.

docs.title: The Vision (verbatim)
docs.text: "I want the app to be like Kodi — the Deck is bare-bones Kodi and from there features can be added or subtracted in an easy and clear way keeping the system clean and fluid." — Anon, 2026-07-07

docs.title: The Platform Architecture
docs.text:
THE DECK (core — bare bones)
├── Auth layer          — ONE password, Cerberus gate, session token propagates
├── Navigation          — tab bar, keyboard shortcuts, module discovery
├── Theme engine        — ThemeNeXuS = DRK-NT palette (Constantine standard)
├── Transaction layer   — everything is a transaction, recorded
└── Module registry     — discovers, loads, and unloads plugins

MODULES (addons — plug in / plug out)
├── DRK-NT              — darknet control (networks, services, Ghost Gate, OpenSnitch)
├── PNG² Editor         — card editor (nexus_png2_editor.py port 7420)
├── AI Sanctum          — characters, Knowledge Graph, Lorebook, Lua, memory
├── Dark-Net-Server     — hosting + production studio (coming soon)
└── [community]         — anyone builds to the module contract

docs.title: The Module Contract (proposed Go interface)
docs.text:
type DeckModule interface {
    ID()      string               // unique module identifier
    TabName() string               // display name in tab bar
    TabKey()  string               // keyboard shortcut
    Init()    tea.Cmd              // startup command
    Update()  (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) // message handler
    View()    string               // render function
}
Modules live in: ~/.config/nexus/deck/modules/ Deck discovers at startup. No hardcoding. No coupling between modules.

docs.title: Critical Principles
docs.text:
One Password — User authenticates ONCE. User struct + EncryptionKey propagates to all modules. Never ask for credentials twice.

Modules Never Know Each Other — Deck is the only coupling point. DRK-NT doesn't import AI Sanctum. PNG² Editor doesn't know Ghost Gate exists.

Three Apps Stay Sovereign — Each app runs standalone OR as a module. Both modes always work.

docs.title: A. ARGUS ACCOUNTABILITY — 🔵 DESIGNED (spec not yet written to a doc; captured in memory)
docs.text:
The mandate (Anon): "Accountability with a cryptographical fingerprint, and everything in NeXuS is a transaction so every transaction will have every fingerprint that touched it."

CIA triad, NeXuS meaning: C=Confidentiality · I=Integrity · A=Accountability (NOT Availability; Availability = "YMC-Availability").

Architecture (all Alpine-repo tools, nothing hand-rolled): - git = the ledger. Every doc/edit/backup = a signed commit. Parent-hash chain = the tamper-evident fingerprint chain. Do NOT build a bespoke PKI/JSONL ledger. - SSH Ed25519 keys = entity identities. git config gpg.format ssh + commit -S + allowed_signers. - Master/child model: ONE master key, password-protected, offline. Master ISSUES children (DERIVED, not certified — chosen because master = sovereign root). One child per entity (anon, claude, eye-sky, node-argus). Only master revokes. Delete = revoke (append, never erase). - KeePass KDBX v2 = vault; Rook (Alpine pkg, sr.ht/~ser/rook) = headless Secret Service serving keys (no GUI). - Keybase sigchain = the pattern we copy, NOT a dependency (Keybase = frozen since Zoom acquisition — the lock-in cautionary tale). - Separate from Ghost Gate key (Ghost Gate = external Nostr kind-24000 receipts). - Two-tier signing: (1) provenance = every op self-signs (frictionless); (2) multi-sig threshold = privileged only (merge to main, backup restore, archive, key changes). - Open integration detail: how Rook (Secret Service = passwords) feeds git's SSH signer (agent vs stored key). Small, testable.

Full detail: memory project_argus_accountability.md.

docs.title: B. WATCHER TAKEDOWN + EMERGENCY STOP LAW — ✅ DONE
docs.text:
• nexus-tmux-watch.sh was a false-positive machine: it flagged our OWN tmux status-bar scripts (continuum_save.sh, ram_info.sh, cpu_info.sh, uptime.sh) as "🔴 UNKNOWN PID ON SOCKET." Log: ~/logs/nexus-tmux-watch.log (25 "alerts" in an hour, all benign).
  • It kept "respawning" because it backgrounds its workers (monitor_loop &, inotifywait … &, line 55/113) → they orphan to PPID 1 and survive killing the launcher. Not resurrection — detached daemons.
  • Killed by exact PID (ps/awk), NOT pkill -f — pkill -f "nexus-tmux-watch" matches our own shell's command line and SIGKILLs it (that was the exit 1/144 bug).
  • Definitive fix: archived the executable → ~/scripts/archive-disabled-2026-07-11/nexus-tmux-watch.sh. Now test -x fails everywhere; no config/orphan can relaunch it. (Line still lives in the sacred backup ~/.config/tmux/org-2026-07-07-tmux.conf:140 but that config isn't sourced and the executable is gone.)
  • Why "why now?" The watcher was only ~5 min old — alerts track the WATCHER'S uptime, not an attacker's arrival. Status bar was always benign; the observer just woke up.

⚖️ EMERGENCY STOP LAW (established this session, in memory feedback_nexus_rules): No power-script (watcher/lockdown/hooks) ships or activates without a working, independent kill switch — preferably a tmux keybinding that nukes hooks + PIDs in one shot. No kill switch = feature doesn't ship.

docs.title: Fossil SCM — evaluated hands-on, leaning ADOPT
docs.text: Fossil v2.28 already installed (/usr/bin/fossil). Answers the parked "is git the best / not so Simple / is gitea the same" question: - git = the VC tool (powerful, not Simple). Gitea = a self-hosted git server/forge — NOT a different/simpler tool, still git underneath. Fossil = a genuinely simpler, self-contained alternative. - Proven facts (all demoed live in ~/Projects/fossil-lab): - 1 .fossil file = 1 whole repo — files + history + wiki + forum + chat + tickets + users, all in one SQLite file. Proved by deleting the working tree and rebuilding it from the file alone. - Working dir = disposable checkout (.fslckout); repo lives in the ONE file (opposite of git's in-tree .git/). Two steps: init/clone the file, then open a checkout. - Empty repo ≈ 212K = fixed forge-schema overhead (27 tables). Text compresses + deltas; binaries bloat it — keep out (matches CLAUDE.md no-binaries rule). - Simpler than git: no staging/index dance — commit auto-includes tracked edits; add only for NEW files. Has fossil undo (reverses last update/merge/revert — git has no equivalent). - Not a walled garden: fossil git export maintains an incremental git mirror → still push to GitHub. Fossil = sovereign source of truth, GitHub = mirror. - Zero-install access for others: browse via web UI (browser only); grab code via /tarball/... or /zip/... with plain curl. Only real collaborators need the (tiny, single-binary, zero-dep) install. - Repo list in UI: fossil server ~/museum/ (a DIRECTORY) → root page lists every .fossil = your self-hosted forge homepage. (fossil server repo.fossil = straight into one repo, no list.) CLI: fossil all list (only shows repos opened at least once — dir-server list shows ALL files regardless). - Search: fossil grep PATTERN file = content search across ALL historical versions, no index. Plus FTS5 full-text index (fossil fts-config enable all; index on; reindex) over file content + wiki + forum + tickets + comments → web-UI search box. Use tokenizer trigram for code.

docs.title: Gen6 graphics — VERIFIED working end-to-end
docs.text: Hardware: Dell E6520, Intel Sandy Bridge / HD Graphics 3000 (SNB GT2, Gen6), crocus, OpenGL 3.3 / Mesa 26.1.1. No Vulkan (ANV needs Gen7+). Single Intel GPU, no NVIDIA. - VA-API HW video decode now live: installed libva-intel-driver + libva-utils (Gen6 uses the legacy i965 driver — NOT intel-media-driver, which is Gen8+ and silently won't load). vainfo confirms H.264 (baseline/main/high) + MPEG-2 decode (+H.264 encode). - ~/.config/mpv/mpv.conf: hwdec=no → hwdec=vaapi, vo=gpu. Tested: an h264 940x1280 clip played clean, no garbage, LOW CPU (= real GPU offload). This build has no dmabuf-wl vo — use gpu/gpu-next on Wayland, drm on bare TTY. - ~/.config/fish/conf.d/nexus-graphics.fish (NEW): exports LIBVA_DRIVER_NAME=i965, MESA_GLTHREAD=true, and CHROMIUM_USER_FLAGS. - nexus-wayland-launcher.sh: WLR_NO_HARDWARE_CURSORS is now NVIDIA-only → Intel gets hardware cursors. Also added foot --server startup (see below). - RAM = nothing to do: nexus-dmi-mem.py read it safely → 4 GB ChannelA + 8 GB ChannelB @ 1333 MT/s = dual-channel FLEX (8 GB interleaved full-bandwidth + 4 GB single). 1333 is the SNB max. Fully-symmetric would need 2×8 GB (marginal iGPU gain — not worth $).

docs.title: Chromium garbage — FIXED (Firefox was always fine)
docs.text: chrome://gpu dump (~/Downloads/about-gpu-2026-07-20*.txt) showed Chromium on ANGLE→OpenGL ES 3.0 on crocus with Rasterization: Hardware accelerated — HW raster on SNB paints garbage. Fix persisted in nexus-graphics.fish: set -gx CHROMIUM_USER_FLAGS "--disable-gpu-rasterization" (Alpine chromium wrapper appends CHROMIUM_USER_FLAGS — no root). Keeps HW compositing + HW video decode; only raster → CPU. Anon confirmed clean. (Launcher/fuzzel-spawned chromium needs next Wayland session to inherit the env; terminal-launched picks it up now.)

docs.title: apk world hygiene — 4 errors → 3 benign, NO force, NO cascade damage
docs.text: Root cause of "all sink installs failing": a dirty apk world made apk exit non-zero on every op; the sink misread that as per-package conflict. - Removed apk-snap (btrfs commit-hook) — root is ext4-on-LVM, so it errored every apk run + spammed subvolume is not a btrfs. Cascaded out snapper + btrfs-progs-libs (dead weight); btrfs-progs tools kept (no btrfs mounts anywhere; sdb1 3.6T unformatted). - incus flavor collision FIXED: had both incus-openrc (LTS) and incus-feature-openrc installed → both own /etc/init.d/incusd. Removed the mismatched incus-feature-openrc (init for a incus-feature daemon that isn't installed); incus-openrc now owns incusd, matching the installed LTS incus. - 3 benign collisions LEFT baselined (removing cascades badly): 3proxy-doc⨯libproxy-doc, outils-doc⨯uutils-coreutils-doc, and freeradius-client⨯ppp-radius — the RADIUS one is STUCK because removing freeradius-client cascades to 58 packages (nagios-plugins-all → all nagios plugins + net-snmp). Deliberately not touched. - Discipline throughout: apk del -s simulate before every delete, never --force (Anon's hard rule: force/override "cripples a system for life").

docs.title: nexus-apk-sink.sh — HARDENED for a dirty world (backup .bak-20260719_183534)
docs.text: (1) baseline pre-existing apk error-lines via apk add --simulate busybox; (2) flag a pkg as conflict only if it emits MORE errors than baseline (not on exit code); (3) judge install success by apk info -e STATE not exit code. Result: netscanner sink then walked all 33 pkgs, 0 conflict / 0 dropped.

docs.title: Encryption Architecture (designed, not yet implemented)
docs.text:
User Password → PBKDF2 → User Master Key (AES-256-GCM) — BOSS
    ↓ HKDF(master + char_id)
Character Key (revocable — revoke = re-encrypt with new derivation)
    ↓
Session Key (random per new chat, encrypted with User Master Key)
    ↓ encrypts
Chat messages, memory written in session
- Multi-char sessions: one session key (user domain), character keys for per-char files only - hiddenFrom[] field handles per-recipient access control at session layer (not crypto) - Summary hash chain: tamper-detection, integrity (from Perchance Amy blueprint) - Export/share: plain OR transfer-password; recipient re-encrypts with own password - Standard primitive: AES-256-GCM (Go char-gen already uses this — correct) - Python Fernet (AES-128) must be upgraded to AES-256-GCM for compatibility

Session Overview

  • fprintd — VFS5011 hardware detected but flaky driver, nothing enrolled. Not stable enough for PAM auth.
  • ossec-hids — BROKEN partial install. Only ossec-execd + ossec-monitord running. Missing analysisd/logcollector/syscheckd. Effectively dead.

Track 1 — Go CLI (nexus-cli) - Ghost Gate, Observer, Dark Stack protocol daemons - Character reader with notcurses true pixel rendering - Long-running services, systems code - cage-foot native, runs anywhere, no browser

Track 2 — Python + TS/JS Web (nexus-web) - Web server + API proxy (already built) - Full image rendering, rich UI - Browser interface, served by nexus_web_server.py

Same character cards, same API backend, same provider stack. Different rendering surface. Web suite is the bridge making both feel like one system.

docs.title: The Two Modes
docs.text:
Mode 1 — CLI Pure (Ghost/Headless)
  kmscon → tuios/tmux → micro + yazi + w3m + foot-server
  No compositor, boots in seconds, lowest attack surface

Mode 2 — Minimal Wayland (Operator)
  cage → foot-client (connects to foot-server)
  Terminal IS the desktop, cage is ~500 lines C, invisible infrastructure

docs.title: Community Editions
docs.text:
CE-0   CLI-Pure       kmscon + tmux(v1)/tuios(v2) + TUI stack
CE-1   Cage           CE-0 + cage + foot server/client
CE-2   labwc          CE-1 + labwc + thunar + standard apps
CE-3   labwc-qs       CE-2 + quickshell + full NeXuS HUD

Each is strict superset of previous. Drop down any tier.

docs.title: Multiplexer Decision
docs.text:
v1 first adopters  →  tmux default (power users, muscle memory)
v2 broader base    →  tuios default (friendlier, "Terminal UI OS" framing)
tmux always available as swap

Tuios = "Terminal UI Operating System" — mouse, workspaces, tiling, Nerd Font icons, 11MB. First adopters ARE power users (sysadmins, Arch reddit crowd). Friendliness is a v2 problem.

docs.title: The Wayland Decision — Settled
docs.text:
• NO X11: hard line, always was
  • Wayland: correct engineering conclusion after living the alternatives
  • kmscon framebuffer path: looks minimal, actually insecure (broad /dev/fb0 permissions, less audited)
  • cage + foot: proper Wayland isolation, better security MODEL than raw KMS

"CLI purists complaining about Wayland are running Hyprland with 47 widgets. Their 'CLI only' is a terminal inside a GUI. NeXuS CLI is actually CLI only."

docs.title: foot sings in cage
docs.text:
• Direct path: foot → cage → KMS → display
  • foot server/client: instant spawn, shared memory, no per-window overhead
  • No compositor overhead stealing cycles
  • Better rendering than kmscon: faster, more color, sixel native

docs.title: App Registry · NNCC · Security HUD · Timeline Additions
docs.text:
Session type: Infrastructure + Integration Status: ✅ TESTED — all changes live and verified Written by: Claude (Sonnet 4.6) + Anon

Think of this compass like an instruction manual. Every change is explained: what it is, why we did it, and how it works. If you read this, you should be able to understand everything that happened today — even if you weren't there.

docs.title: What broke
docs.text:
The NeXuS Dashboard uses a program called wtfutil to show a live info panel. When you ran the launch script, it said: 

Command /home/user/.config/wtf/config.yml is not supported

docs.title: Why it broke
docs.text:
The launch script was starting wtfutil like this: 

wtfutil -c ~/.config/wtf/config.yml
The -c flag with a space after it is the OLD way. The version of wtfutil installed on this machine is a "dev" build that only accepts the flag written like this: 
wtfutil --config="/home/user/.config/wtf/config.yml"
When it saw -c with a space, it thought the file path was a command name. It was confused.

docs.title: What we changed
docs.text:
File: ~/scripts/nexus-dashboard.sh

Old line: 

exec /usr/bin/wtfutil -c ~/.config/wtf/config.yml

New line: 

exec /usr/bin/wtfutil --config="${HOME}/.config/wtf/config.yml"

Two things changed: the flag name (long form --config= instead of -c), and the path uses $HOME instead of ~ (more reliable in scripts).

docs.title: 🛡️ FIX 2 — OSSEC Not Wired Into Security HUD
What was missing
docs.text: The Security HUD (~/scripts/nexus-security-hud.sh) watches for intruders and shows alerts. It was supposed to read from OSSEC (our host intrusion detector), but the OSSEC block was completely missing from the code. The HUD watched for PSAD, Suricata, and Fail2ban — but silently ignored OSSEC entirely.

docs.title: Why OSSEC is tricky
docs.text:
OSSEC saves its alert log at /var/ossec/logs/alerts/alerts.log but only root can read it. Regular users can't open that file.

The solution: the user account is in the wheel group, and /var/log/messages is readable by wheel. OSSEC writes there too. Even better, we can add the user to the ossecr group (OSSEC's read-only group) to read the alerts file directly.

docs.title: What we added
docs.text:
File: ~/scripts/nexus-security-hud.sh

We added a new block inside the check_alerts() function. It: 1. Tries to read the last 30 lines of the OSSEC alerts log 2. Pulls out: the source IP (srcip:), the alert level (a number 1-15), and the rule description 3. If level is 10 or above → RED threat. Below 10 → ORANGE. 4. Alerts without a source IP (like file integrity checks) just appear in the feed without raising the threat level 5. If the log file can't be read at all, it shows a one-time warning in the feed so you know OSSEC isn't connected

docs.title: How to fully activate OSSEC in the HUD
docs.text:
Run this (needs a TTY): 

doas addgroup user ossecr
Then log out and back in. After that, the HUD reads OSSEC alerts automatically.

docs.title: 🏗️ BUILD 5 — The App Registry (The Big Fix)
The problem we were solving
docs.text: Every time we wanted to add a new app to the NeXuS web server, someone had to write new Python code. If you wanted /nncc/ to work, you'd add an if path == '/nncc/': block. If you wanted /search/ to work, another block. This is called "hardcoding" — it's like having to rebuild your house every time you want a new door.

docs.title: The solution: a registry
docs.text:
Instead of writing code for each app, we made the web server read a list of apps from environment variables. Think of it like a phone book — you just add a name and number to the book, and calls get routed automatically.

How it works: In ~/NeXuS/secrets/nexus.env, you add three lines per app: 

NEXUS_APP_NNCC_prefix=/nncc          # what URL it lives at
NEXUS_APP_NNCC_static=/path/to/files # where its web files are (optional)
NEXUS_APP_NNCC_backend=http://127.0.0.1:8801  # where its API is (optional)
NEXUS_APP_NNCC_api_prefix=/api       # only proxy paths that start with this (optional)

When the web server starts, it reads all the NEXUS_APP_* lines and builds a routing table automatically. To add a new app: add three lines, restart the server. No code changes. Ever.

docs.title: What the routing logic does
docs.text:
When a request comes in for /nncc/api/networks: 1. Server checks: does any registered app have a prefix that matches /nncc? Yes — NNCC. 2. What's left after removing /nncc? → /api/networks 3. Does /api/networks start with the api_prefix /api? Yes → proxy to backend. 4. Makes a request to http://127.0.0.1:8801/api/networks and returns the result.

When a request comes in for /nncc/css/nexus.css: 1. Matches NNCC. 2. What's left? → /css/nexus.css 3. Does it start with /api? No → serve static file. 4. Opens ~/nexus-network/web/css/nexus.css and sends it to the browser.

• ~/Projects/nexus-web-server/nexus_web_server.py — added _build_app_registry(), _match_registry(), _dispatch_registry(), _registry_proxy(), _registry_static(). Also added do_PATCH(), do_DELETE(), do_PUT() handlers.

docs.title: The bug we hit (and fixed)
docs.text:
The registry was reading os.environ (the system environment variables), but nexus.env isn't in the system environment — the web server reads it itself using its own _env_dict() function. So at startup, when the registry was built, the nexus.env vars hadn't been read yet.

Fix: Changed _build_app_registry() to use _env_dict() which reads nexus.env directly, merged with any system env vars: 

env = {**_env_dict(), **os.environ}  # nexus.env first, process env wins

docs.title: 🌐 BUILD 6 — NNCC Wired Into NeXuS Web Server
What NNCC is
docs.text:
The NeXuS Network Command Center (NNCC) is a dashboard for controlling darknet services: Tor, I2P, Yggdrasil, Reticulum, IPFS, Snowflake. It has: - A frontend (web UI at ~/nexus-network/web/) — the pretty dashboard you see - A backend (FastAPI server at :8801) — the brains that actually talks to the services

Before today, the UI was served by a bare python3 -m http.server on port 8880. After today, everything goes through the NeXuS web server.

docs.title: Changes to the frontend (app.js)
docs.text:
The JavaScript used to hardcode http://127.0.0.1:8801 everywhere — the address of the backend API. This is like telling everyone "our office is at 123 Main St" but then moving the office and having to tell everyone the new address.

We changed it to be smart about where it is: 

const _NNCC_PREFIX = window.location.pathname.startsWith('/nncc') ? '/nncc' : '';
const API_BASE = window.location.origin + _NNCC_PREFIX;

Translation: "If this page is being served from /nncc/, add /nncc to all API calls. If it's being served directly (like the old way), don't add anything."

This means the NNCC works whether served from the NeXuS web server OR from the old standalone server — one codebase, two deployment options.

docs.title: The nexus-nncc.sh management script
docs.text:
We wrote a new script (~/scripts/nexus-nncc.sh) to manage the NNCC backend, following the same pattern as nexus-api-proxy.sh. Commands: 

nexus-nncc.sh start    # start the API in a tmux session
nexus-nncc.sh stop     # stop it
nexus-nncc.sh restart  # stop then start
nexus-nncc.sh logs     # attach to the tmux session to see live output
nexus-nncc.sh status   # show what's running and whether the API responds

The script also: - Checks that the venv exists before trying to start - Waits up to 15 seconds for the API to respond before declaring failure - Self-backs up on every launch (NeXuS standard) - Uses env vars for paths (no hardcoding)

docs.title: Bugs we hit and fixed
docs.text:
Bug 1: Wrong path in start-nncc.sh The old startup script had a hardcoded path: 

COMMAND_CENTER="/home/user/claude/configs/nexus-stack/command-center"
But the actual backend lives at ~/Projects/nexus-network-stack/command-center/. Fixed to use an env var with a sensible default: 
COMMAND_CENTER="${NEXUS_NNCC_DIR:-${HOME}/Projects/nexus-network-stack/command-center}"

Bug 2: exec with a pipe breaks logging The nexus-nncc.sh script used exec uvicorn ... | tee logfile. The exec command replaces the shell process — so the pipe to tee gets orphaned. The log file stays empty. Fixed by removing exec: 

# broken:
exec '$UVICORN' main:app ... 2>&1 | tee '$LOG_FILE'
# fixed:
'$UVICORN' main:app ... 2>&1 | tee '$LOG_FILE'; read

Bug 3: Hardcoded data path in config.py The NNCC backend's config had: 

data_dir: Path = Path("/home/user/claude/configs/nexus-stack")
But /home/user/claude/configs/nexus-stack already exists as a file — not a directory. When the backend tried to create it as a directory, it failed. Fixed to use the NeXuS standard location: 
data_dir: Path = Path.home() / "NeXuS" / "data" / "nncc"
Also created ~/NeXuS/data/nncc/ so it exists before the server starts.

Bug 4: Python 3.14 vs pydantic-core The requirements.txt pinned pydantic==2.5.3 which requires pydantic-core==2.14.6. But the system runs Python 3.14, and pydantic-core 2.14.6 was written before Python 3.14 existed. A Python 3.14 API change (ForwardRef._evaluate() needs a recursive_guard argument now) causes the Rust build to fail with a Python error.

Fixed by unpinning pydantic and requiring a minimum version: 

pydantic>=2.8.0   # was: pydantic==2.5.3
Pydantic 2.8+ supports Python 3.14 and has pre-built binary wheels (no compilation needed).

docs.title: 🔑 KEY LESSONS FROM TODAY
docs.text:
1. Registry over hardcoding. When you find yourself writing the same pattern more than twice (if path == '/this', if path == '/that'), stop and make it data-driven. The App Registry is the NeXuS solution: one pattern, all apps, config in nexus.env.

2. Check where env vars come from. Python's os.environ only has what the shell passes in. If your program loads secrets from a file, make sure the code that READS those secrets uses the same file-reading function, not os.environ directly.

3. exec with a pipe is a trap. exec replaces the current process. If you pipe exec ... | something, the pipe's right side never connects properly. Use the command without exec when you need piping.

4. Python version matters for Rust packages. Packages like pydantic-core compile Rust code against the Python C API. When Python 3.14 changed an internal API, old versions of pydantic-core broke. The fix: don't pin to exact versions of Rust-based packages — use >= and let pip find a version with pre-built wheels for your Python.

docs.title: nexus-wiki-publish.sh
docs.text:
File: ~/scripts/nexus-wiki-publish.sh

What it syncs: - All <project>/docs/action_report.md → ~/git/nexus/docs/reports/<project>.md (25 found) - ~/NeXuS/timeline/NEXUS_TIMELINE.md → ~/git/nexus/docs/timeline.md - All ~/NeXuS/timeline/compass/*.md → ~/git/nexus/docs/compass/ (23 synced) - Generates ~/git/nexus/docs/reports/index.md with table of all projects - Updates ~/git/nexus/mkdocs.yml nav — inserts Reports + Session Compass sections between markers

Markers in mkdocs.yml: 

# --- NEXUS-WIKI-AUTO-START ---
  - Timeline: timeline.md
  - Reports: ...
  - Session Compass: ...
# --- NEXUS-WIKI-AUTO-END ---
Safe to run repeatedly — idempotent, updates between markers without touching rest of nav.
