def calculate_daily_token_release(network_state):
    total_nodes = network_state.node_count
    total_resources = network_state.storage_gb + network_state.bandwidth_mbps
    network_usage = network_state.transactions_per_day

    base_release = sqrt(total_nodes * total_resources)
    usage_multiplier = log(network_usage + 1)

    return base_release * usage_multiplier

def calculate_token_value(network_state, circulating_supply):
    network_asset_value = (
        network_state.storage_gb * storage_market_rate +
        network_state.bandwidth_tb * bandwidth_market_rate +
        network_state.cpu_hours * cpu_market_rate
    )
    return network_asset_value / circulating_supply

docs.text:
Goal: Break it BEFORE users do

Test Scenarios:

a) High Load - 1,000+ concurrent connections - Saturate bandwidth - Max out CPU routing decisions - Find breaking point

b) Network Chaos - Kill Tor randomly (does failover work?) - Kill I2P mid-transfer (does it recover?) - Kill ALL networks then bring back (does it heal?) - Rapid cycling (stress failover logic)

c) Peer Churn - Nodes joining/leaving constantly - Mesh network instability - B.A.T.M.A.N./Yggdrasil peer discovery under chaos

d) Latency Hell - Simulate 5000ms latency (Tor over satellite) - Network congestion, packet loss - Does health monitoring handle slow networks?

e) DDoS Simulation - Flood with requests - Resource exhaustion - Memory leaks (run 24 hours)

f) Edge Cases - Malformed requests - Unknown protocols - Circular routing (A→B→A loops) - DNS poisoning attempts

g) AI Decision Testing - Test pattern recognition accuracy - Emergency fallback (kill internet → Meshtastic?) - AI routing under load - Verify no AI decision causes failure

Tools: - ab (Apache Bench) - HTTP load testing - iperf3 - Bandwidth saturation - tc (traffic control) - Simulate latency/packet loss - Custom chaos scripts - Kill networks randomly - stress-ng - CPU/memory exhaustion

Success Criteria: - Handles 1,000+ connections without crash - Failover works under load - Recovers from all network failures - No memory leaks (24-hour run) - Graceful degradation (slow, not broken) - AI decisions don't cause failures

Bell Labs Vision:

"Your CPU can be in California, your storage in New York, your display in Tokyo. The network makes it all one system."

Key Principles: - Everything is a file - Network transparency - Distributed by design - Simple, elegant, composable - No central servers

What Happened: - ✅ Technology succeeded (9P protocol, ideas spread) - ❌ Adoption failed (too radical for corporate IT) - ❌ Ideas stolen (cloud companies = Plan 9 + surveillance) - ❌ Users lost (AWS/Google = Plan 9 philosophy, centralized control)

Why It Failed: - Too different from Unix (scared users away) - No killer app (technically superior ≠ market success) - Poor timing (1992 networks too slow) - No commercial backing (AT&T breakup)

docs.title: Napster (1999): Peer-to-Peer Sharing
docs.text:
Shawn Fanning's Vision:

"Your music collection is my music collection. Share everything with everyone. No central storage, just a community of peers."

Key Principles: - Peer-to-peer file sharing - No central storage (just index) - Everyone contributes - Community collaboration - Information wants to be free

What Happened: - ✅ Technology succeeded (P2P works!) - ❌ Legally destroyed (RIAA lawsuit, 2001) - ❌ Replaced by centralization (iTunes, Spotify) - ❌ Users lost (subscriptions instead of ownership) - ❌ Sharing became "piracy" (criminalized)

Why It Failed: - Central index = single point of failure (legal target) - Record labels sued it to death - Replaced with "legal" alternatives (DRM, streaming) - Users traded freedom for convenience

docs.title: How Centralized Powers Kill Decentralization
docs.text:
Stage 1: Innovation Emerges - Bitcoin: Decentralized money invented - Plan 9: Distributed computing demonstrated - Napster: Peer-to-peer sharing works

Stage 2: Threat Recognized - Bitcoin: Banks see threat to their monopoly - Plan 9: Corporate IT sees threat to control - Napster: Record labels see threat to revenue

Stage 3: Attack or Ignore - Bitcoin: Can't shut down (no central server) → capture it instead - Plan 9: Too radical → ignore it, steal ideas later - Napster: Central index → easy legal target → shut down

Stage 4: Centralization Restored - Bitcoin → Centralized exchanges (Coinbase, Binance) + KYC - Plan 9 → Cloud computing (AWS, Google) + surveillance - Napster → Streaming services (Spotify, Apple) + subscriptions

Stage 5: Users Lose - Bitcoin users: Surveillance, fees, no privacy - Plan 9 users: Vendor lock-in, no freedom - Napster users: No ownership, monthly fees

  • Plan 9: Distributed computing, centralized adoption = FAILED
  • Napster: Peer-to-peer files, central index = FAILED

docs.title: 🔥 CRITICAL MEMORY LEAK FIX - Terminal Crash Resolution
docs.text: Date: 2026-02-12 Session: Terminal Access & AI Bridge Enhancement Location: /home/user/Projects/adv-ai-nexus/advanced-ai-character-generator-terminal-access

docs.title: Problem Identified
docs.text:
Characters using the terminal caused tab crashes due to severe memory leaks:

  1. JSON Deep Clone Hell: Every terminal command executed JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(state)) creating massive memory copies
  2. Unbounded History Growth: Command history grew infinitely with no size limits
  3. UI History Bloat: Terminal window kept unlimited output history

  • ✅ Implemented structural sharing for filesystem tree

docs.text:

  • After: Shallow copy with selective deep clone (~100KB for mutations)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Successfully implemented a comprehensive fix for the 429 "Too Many Requests" error that was occurring with Google's Generative Language API.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
The application was experiencing 429 errors when making API calls to Google's API: 

09:14:26 | ERROR | core.models | API Request Error (google): 429 Client Error: Too Many Requests
requests.exceptions.HTTPError: 429 Client Error: Too Many Requests

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text: The call_api method in core/models.py was making direct HTTP requests without: - Retry logic for transient errors - Exponential backoff between retries - Provider-specific error handling - Support for Retry-After headers

docs.title: 1. Added Retry Strategy with Exponential Backoff
docs.text:
• 5 retry attempts for 429 errors
  • Exponential backoff: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 seconds
  • Status codes handled: 429, 500, 502, 503, 504
  • Respect Retry-After headers from API

docs.title: 2. Enhanced Error Handling
docs.text:
• Provider-specific messages: Google, Mistral, OpenAI get tailored messages
  • User-friendly responses: Clear guidance on what to do
  • Graceful degradation: Helpful messages when retries exhausted

docs.title: 3. Technical Implementation
docs.text:
• Added required imports: HTTPAdapter, Retry
  • Implemented session-based requests with retry strategy
  • Added comprehensive 429 error handling in multiple locations
  • Proper session cleanup with finally block

docs.title: Key Improvements
docs.text: ✅ Automatic Retries: 5 attempts with exponential backoff ✅ Provider-Specific Messages: Tailored error messages for each provider ✅ Retry-After Support: Respects API's suggested wait time ✅ Better UX: Clear, actionable error messages for users ✅ Robust Error Handling: Catches 429 errors in multiple places ✅ Backward Compatible: No breaking changes to existing functionality

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Created comprehensive test suite (test_429_fix.py) that verifies: - ✅ Retry logic implementation with exponential backoff - ✅ 429 error handling with user-friendly messages - ✅ Provider-specific error messages (Google, Mistral, OpenAI) - ✅ Retry-After header support - ✅ Graceful error handling when retries exhausted

All tests passed! 🎉

docs.title: Files Modified
docs.text:
1. core/models.py - Enhanced API calling with retry logic and 429 error handling
  2. test_429_fix.py - Comprehensive test suite for the fix
  3. docs/action_reports/google_429_fix.md - Detailed documentation

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• ✅ Existing tests still pass (6/7 - 1 expected failure due to missing API key)
  • ✅ New functionality works correctly
  • ✅ No breaking changes introduced
  • ✅ Better user experience confirmed

docs.title: Before Fix
docs.text:
User: "Hello, how are you?"
AI: "An unexpected error occurred while processing your request. Please try again."
Logs: "429 Client Error: Too Many Requests"

docs.title: After Fix
docs.text:
User: "Hello, how are you?"
AI: "Google API rate limit exceeded. Please try again in 30 seconds."
Logs: "Rate limited by google API. Retry-After: 30"

Status: RESOLVED 🎉

The fix provides automatic recovery from rate limits with exponential backoff, provider-specific error messages, and graceful degradation when limits are reached.

docs.title: DIVA Chain Integration Design - Multi-Chain I2P-Native Seeding Layer (2026-02-20 14:24)
docs.text:
What: Designed DIVA chain integration as the anonymous seeding and discovery backbone for the full NeXuS stack.

Why: Need a decentralized node registry with zero clearnet exposure. Existing solutions require central servers or expose metadata. DIVA chain is I2P-native and battle-tested (successor to Konrad's original chain which was deanonymized reproducibly).

How: DIVA is multi-chain, born inside I2P, never touches clearnet. Node bootstrap: I2P tunnels build (10-30 min) then node reads chain for peer list, cipher manifests (IPFS hashes), profile hashes, relay pool membership. Node announces itself with only master pubkey + cryptographic proof of work - no name, no IP, no identity. Ephemeral rotating API tokens (3-10 min). Native XMR/BTC bridge built in. Two-layer key architecture: cold master key (Ed25519) signs rotating hot session keys (BIP32-derived). Contacts look up master pubkey, chain returns current session key signed by master. Balances sweep through XMR ring sigs before session wallet burns.

Files: docs/action_report.md, ROADMAP.md (nexus-phantom)

Dependencies: I2P (SAM protocol), IPFS, Monero

docs.title: Fixed greetd login manager + added NeXuS terminal sessions (2026-02-21)
docs.text:
What: Diagnosed greetd crash, fixed config, removed tor autostart, added two new beautiful terminal sessions to the NeXuS login screen.

Why: greetd was crashing on boot because /etc/inittab had a getty respawning on tty1 (conflicting with greetd owning VT1), and the session-wrapper path used ~ which doesn't expand for the system greeter user (no home dir). User also wanted tor removed from startup and a way to get back the beautiful terminal experience previously seen via slim.

Root Causes Fixed:

  1. greetd crash — /etc/inittab tty1::respawn:getty fought greetd for VT1. Fix: apply.sh now comments out the tty1 getty line.
  2. ~ in config.toml — --session-wrapper '~/.local/bin/sway-session-wrapper' resolved to wrong path for greeter system user. Fix: changed to absolute /home/user/.local/bin/sway-session-wrapper.
  3. slim conflict — slim was still running alongside greetd. Fix: apply.sh now stops and disables slim too.
  4. tor autostart — removed from default runlevel via apply.sh.

Keyboard mystery solved: When slim (X11 DM) launched the CLI session (Exec=/bin/zsh -l), it ran zsh inside X11 with no terminal window — keyboard events went to X's focused client (nothing). docs.title: Fixed nexus-medusa.sh -- podman --replace flag (2026-03-07 18:05)
docs.text:
What: Added --replace flag to both podman run calls in nexus-medusa.sh to prevent "name already in use" container conflicts.

Why: When Medusa tried to launch a container with a name that already existed (stopped, crashed, or orphaned), Podman would error with "that name is already used". The script had manual cleanup code (podman stop + podman rm -f) above the run call but race conditions or partial failures could still leave the name occupied.

How: Added --replace to both podman run invocations:

Line 190 — main container launch: ```bash

docs.title: Before:
docs.text: cid=$(podman run -d --rm --name "$name" \

docs.title: After:
docs.text:
cid=$(podman run -d --rm --replace --name "$name" \ ```

Line 789 — relay container launch: ```bash

docs.title: Before:
docs.text: podman run -d --rm --name "$relay_name" \

docs.title: After:
docs.text:
podman run -d --rm --replace --name "$relay_name" \ ```

--replace atomically stops and removes any existing container with the same name before creating the new one. The existing manual cleanup code above line 190 was left intact — no features removed.

Files: - /home/user/scripts/nexus-medusa.sh — patched - /home/user/scripts/nexus-medusa.sh.bak.* — timestamped backup

What: Fixed nexus-wifi.sh WiFi switcher script — was throwing 'invalid field' and 'invalid parameter' errors making it non-functional.

Why: Script had 3 distinct bugs that prevented connecting to saved networks and disconnecting from WiFi.

How:

Bug 1 — nmcli invalid field error: - Problem: nmcli -t -f NAME,802-11-wireless.ssid connection show throws 'Error: invalid field 802-11-wireless.ssid' because 802-11-wireless.ssid is not a valid list-mode field, only a per-profile field - Fix: Changed connect_to() to loop through saved profiles individually, querying each with nmcli connection show <profile> to read 802-11-wireless.ssid per-profile, then match against the target SSID

Bug 2 — hardcoded wlan0 device name: - Problem: --disconnect flag had local wifi_dev declared inside a case block (invalid in bash) and hardcoded 'wlan0' which fails on systems with different interface names (wlp2s0, wlan1, etc.) - Fix: Detect device dynamically: nmcli -t -f DEVICE,TYPE device status | grep ':wifi:' | cut -d: -f1 | head -1

Bug 3 — fzf reload bind ioctl error: - Problem: --bind ctrl-r:reload(...) had a sleep 2 inside the reload command. fzf executes reload commands in a subshell with no TTY, so sleep throws 'Inappropriate ioctl for device' - Fix: Removed sleep from the fzf reload bind entirely (rescan itself takes a moment anyway)

Dependencies: nmcli, fzf

docs.title: Fix UFW+PSAD logging chain (klogd missing) (2026-03-09 21:55)
docs.text:
What: Fixed broken logging chain preventing PSAD from ever detecting port scans.

Why: PSAD was running for months but had never detected a single packet. Three separate failures in the chain made it completely blind.

Root Causes Found (in order of investigation): 1. klogd not running — iptables LOG entries go to kernel ring buffer only. Without klogd reading /proc/kmsg and forwarding to syslogd, firewall events never reach /var/log/messages. klogd was installed but stopped, not in any runlevel. 2. before.rules LOG rules had no --log-prefix — even if klogd ran, PSAD couldn't identify firewall entries vs other kernel messages. Rules were: -A INPUT -j LOG (all traffic, no prefix, wrong chain). 3. psad.conf SYSLOG_DAEMON set to 'metalog' — but metalog is not running. Busybox syslogd (/sbin/syslogd) is the actual daemon. 4. metalog.conf had a syntax error in the fail2ban section (missing closing quote on logdir line) — not actively harmful since metalog is not running, but fixed for correctness.

How: - Diagnosed by: checking lsmod (ip_tables 0 refs, xt_LOG 22 refs = rules loaded but logs going nowhere), checking ps (no klogd), checking /var/log/messages (no kern.* entries at all), checking rc-status (syslog = busybox syslogd). - Fix script created: ~/scripts/nexus-fix-psad-logging.sh (run with: doas sh ~/scripts/nexus-fix-psad-logging.sh)

Files: - ~/scripts/nexus-fix-psad-logging.sh — fix script (backups, all 4 fixes, service restarts) - /etc/ufw/before.rules — LOG rules get [UFW BLOCK] prefix + moved to ufw-before-input chain - /etc/psad/psad.conf — SYSLOG_DAEMON changed to syslogd, IPT_PREFIX=[UFW BLOCK] added - /etc/metalog.conf — fail2ban logdir syntax error fixed - /etc/conf.d/klogd — klogd added to boot runlevel

To apply: doas sh ~/scripts/nexus-fix-psad-logging.sh To verify: grep 'UFW BLOCK' /var/log/messages && psad --Status

docs.title: Fix fwsnort iptables-nft port negation incompatibility (2026-03-09 22:20)
docs.text:
What: Fixed fwsnort failing to load 29,680 rules due to 8 lines with invalid iptables-nft port negation syntax.

Why: iptables-restore v1.8.11 (nf_tables) rejects rules where ! appears inside a multiport comma-separated list (e.g. --dports 25,!445,!1500). This caused the entire fwsnort ruleset to fail at line 19885, leaving zero snort-based detection active.

Root cause: fwsnort incorrectly translates some Snort port negation rules into multiport lists with ! inside the values. This is a fwsnort translation bug - the syntax was tolerated by legacy iptables but rejected by nftables backend.

How: Identified 8 bad command lines out of 29,680 total (grep 'dports.*,![0-9]'). Strip those lines with sed before applying rules. The 8 removed rules represent untranslatable signatures - removing them is safer than corrupting the match logic.

Files created: - ~/scripts/nexus-fix-fwsnort-nftables.sh — strips 8 bad lines, re-applies rules via fwsnort_iptcmds.sh (individual iptables calls, not restore), signals PSAD - ~/scripts/nexus-update-fwsnort.sh — full replacement for /usr/bin/update-fwsnort, includes fix step

To apply now: doas sh ~/scripts/nexus-fix-fwsnort-nftables.sh To make permanent: doas cp ~/scripts/nexus-update-fwsnort.sh /usr/bin/update-fwsnort To verify: doas iptables -L | grep FWSNORT (should show fwsnort chains)

Root cause: Alpine with busybox syslogd routes auth.* facility to /var/log/messages. fail2ban's paths-common.conf defaults sshd_log to /var/log/auth.log which does not exist. The jail.d override was pointing to /var/log/sshd_log which is also empty.

Also confirmed: PermitRootLogin no already set in /etc/ssh/sshd_config — root SSH login already disabled.

How: Fix logpath in jail.d/alpine-ssh.conf + create paths-overrides.local for Alpine-correct global default. Also tightened maxretry from 10 to 5.

docs.title: SESSION SUMMARY 2026-03-09/10 — Security stack audit + notes system (2026-03-10 00:03)
docs.text: Session overview: Complete security stack audit. Diagnosed and fixed broken security tools (PSAD, fwsnort, fail2ban all non-functional despite appearing to run). Built CLI notes system in tmux popup.

docs.title: DIAGNOSTIC FINDINGS
docs.text: All three security tools were running but completely non-functional:

docs.title: PSAD — not detecting anything
docs.text:
• Root cause 1: klogd not running. Kernel iptables LOG entries go to /proc/kmsg (kernel ring buffer). Without klogd reading /proc/kmsg and forwarding to syslogd, entries never reach /var/log/messages. klogd binary present at /sbin/klogd but status=stopped, not in any runlevel.
  • Root cause 2: UFW before.rules had -A INPUT -j LOG and -A FORWARD -j LOG with NO --log-prefix. PSAD needs a prefix to identify firewall entries vs other kernel messages.
  • Root cause 3: psad.conf had SYSLOG_DAEMON=metalog but metalog is NOT the running syslog daemon. Busybox syslogd (/sbin/syslogd -t -n) is the actual daemon.
  • Root cause 4: metalog.conf had broken fail2ban section syntax (logdir = "/var/log/ missing closing quote and path) — not harmful since metalog not running but fixed for correctness.
  • Confirmed via: lsmod showing xt_LOG with 22 refs (rules active) but ip_tables with 0 refs; ps showing no klogd; /var/log/messages having zero kern.* entries; /var/log/ufw.log empty since Jan 2025.

docs.title: fwsnort — rules never loaded
docs.text:
• Root cause: fwsnort generates some rules with ! inside multiport port lists (e.g. --dports 25,!445,!1500). This is invalid syntax for iptables v1.8.11 (nf_tables backend). iptables-restore rejects the ENTIRE 29,672-rule ruleset at line 19885.
  • Scale: only 8 bad lines out of 29,672. All other rules valid.
  • Rules were last generated/attempted July 24 2025 — 7+ months stale.
  • Daily cron at /etc/periodic/daily/fwsnort exists but no root crontab entry for run-parts — daily updates never ran.
  • Confirmed via: grep 'dports.*,![0-9]' fwsnort_iptcmds.sh returning 8 hits.

docs.title: fail2ban — watching empty file
docs.text:
• Root cause: logpath in jail.d/alpine-ssh.conf pointed to /var/log/sshd_log (0 bytes, never written, created Jan 2025).
  • The correct path (/var/log/messages) was already commented out in the config file — someone knew the fix but left it inactive.
  • paths-common.conf defaults sshd_log to /var/log/auth.log which doesn't exist on Alpine with busybox syslogd.
  • auth.* facility routes to /var/log/messages on this system (confirmed with logger -p auth.info test).
  • fail2ban was running, jails started, pyinotify watching — just watching the wrong empty file.
  • Also confirmed: PermitRootLogin no already set in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.

User customises with wipe/notify/lockdown actions. - nexus-time-setup.sh: 17-option interactive menu. Live status indicators in menu header. Scriptable via args. - Fixed 'Cannot talk to daemon': original config had cmdport 0 with no bindcmdaddress — both command paths blocked. Fix: removed cmdport 0, added bindcmdaddress 127.0.0.1.

docs.text: Status: ✅ TESTED What: Emergency-stop command that halts NeXuS tmux frames/sessions (the 'stop code') — graceful by default, --hard/--panic on demand. How: Whitelist-only reaper — acts on session names matching frame- or nexus via 'tmux ls'. Graceful path sends C-c to each pane then kill-session; --hard adds pkill -x with a core-process guard (never kills sh/fish/bash/login/tmux/init). Default spares the currently-attached session; --panic includes it. Previews + y/N confirm before killing in default mode. Files: ~/scripts/nexus-halt.sh, ~/scripts/nexus-halt.help.md Testing: Live-fire tested with throwaway sessions (frame-testcli, nexus-scratch, my-real-work). User wanted it transparent, fluid, config-selectable, and re-syncable. SYNC: notcurses can't seek, so [ / ] NUDGE — briefly hold the player that's ahead so the other catches up. nexus-tv-status.sh paints title+progress+vol each -i 1 (fluid). Transparency inherited from foot alpha/blur. NOT yet tested: real sixel playback, yt-dlp stream split, IPC pause/seek/vol/nudge against a live mpv — all need an interactive foot session with a wallpaper/display. docs.title: Hardened nexus-apk-sink — tolerate a dirty apk world (2026-07-20 04:38)
docs.text:
Status: ✅ TESTED (live run installed 33 netscanner pkgs: 0 conflict, 0 dropped)

What: Made the conflict-aware installer robust on machines that already have apk integrity errors. Why: With standing file-collision errors, apk exits non-zero on EVERY op; the sink read that as per-package conflict/failure → user saw 'all installs failing'. How: (1) baseline pre-existing error-lines via 'apk add --simulate busybox'; (2) flag a pkg as conflict only if it emits MORE error lines than baseline (not on raw exit code); (3) judge install success by 'apk info -e' STATE, not exit code (a dirty world makes apk lie). Files: ~/scripts/nexus-apk-sink.sh (backup .bak-20260719_183534). Testing: non-root dry run + live root run walked all 33; conflict/dropped both none. Dependencies: apk; root for --simulate.

docs.text:
Status: ✅ TESTED (apk fix -s: 4 errors → 3 benign; btrfs spam gone)

What: Cleaned partial-upgrade + flavor drift with NO --force and NO destructive cascade. Why: 4 standing apk errors + btrfs snapshot-hook spam on every apk transaction. How: - Removed apk-snap (btrfs commit hook) — root is ext4-on-LVM so it failed every run; cascaded out snapper + btrfs-progs-libs (dead weight on ext4); btrfs-progs TOOLS kept. - incus: removed mismatched incus-feature-openrc (init for a feature daemon not installed); incus-openrc now owns /etc/init.d/incusd, matching the installed LTS incus daemon. - Left 3 benign file-collisions baselined by the hardened sink: 3proxy-doc/libproxy-doc, outils-doc/uutils-coreutils-doc, and freeradius-client/ppp-radius (removal cascades to 58 nagios pkgs — deliberately NOT done). - Method throughout: simulate-before-delete ('apk del -s'), never --force. The 58-pkg simulate is why. Files: system apk db only. Testing: apk fix -s ends at 3 benign errors; no btrfs hook output. Dependencies: apk; root.

docs.text:
Status: ✅ TESTED (user confirmed: clean, no more garbage)

What: Chromium rendered corrupted/garbage on the HD 3000 while Firefox was fine. Why: chrome://gpu showed Chromium using ANGLE→OpenGL ES 3.0 on crocus with 'Rasterization: Hardware accelerated' — HW raster through ANGLE/GLES on Sandy Bridge paints garbage. Firefox uses a different (WebRender/software) path. How: Set CHROMIUM_USER_FLAGS='--disable-gpu-rasterization' in ~/.config/fish/conf.d/nexus-graphics.fish (the Alpine chromium wrapper appends CHROMIUM_USER_FLAGS — no root). Moves rasterization to CPU while KEEPING hardware compositing + hardware video decode (VAAPI). Least-aggressive fix (not --disable-gpu). Files: ~/.config/fish/conf.d/nexus-graphics.fish. Testing: user confirmed clean render after relaunch. Note: launcher(fuzzel)-spawned chromium needs next Wayland session to inherit the env; terminal-launched picks it up immediately. Dependencies: chromium (Alpine wrapper reads /etc/chromium/*.conf + CHROMIUM_USER_FLAGS).

docs.title: 2026-07-24 — Created nexus-vm-forge (TUI VM forge) + Fossil repo
docs.text:
• Status: ✅ TESTED (syntax clean; --help + check verified on host — qemu/qemu-img/KVM/CPU-virt all green). Interactive create/boot flow 🔵 not yet run end-to-end.
  • What: A stupid-simple, dependency-free pure-bash TUI that creates and remembers QEMU/KVM VMs — point at an ISO, enter RAM / cores / disk size / network / CPU-pass, keeps a per-VM registry as the history.

Preflight checks qemu-system-x86_64, qemu-img, /dev/kvm (read/write), and vmx/svm CPU flags, printing distro install one-liners if missing. Remove = archive (config always, disk opt-in), never destroy.

  • nexus-vm-forge.sh — the tool
  • nexus-vm-forge.help.md — help
  • README.md, .gitignore, docs/action_report.md
  • Testing: Not yet exercised: full create → install-from-CD → disk-boot cycle; the none network path; multi-VM port collision (logic in place, unproven). Next real test = re-forge the Artix glibc VM through the TUI.
  • Dependencies: bash, coreutils, qemu-system-x86_64, qemu-img, /dev/kvm (optional; falls back to TCG).

docs.title: NeXuS Scripts
docs.text:
Shell scripts, utilities, and automation tools for the NeXuS node stack.

All scripts follow the NeXuS file protocol: self-identifying names, portable, no hardcoded paths. Environment variables carry all configuration.

docs.title: NCM — Network Connection Manager
docs.text:
Scripts for the nexus-connection-manager — the watchbind TUI and web dashboard for managing interfaces, VPN, and darknet services.

Script Purpose nexus-ncm-certs.sh mTLS client certificate manager — issue, revoke, and install browser certs for the NCM web dashboard

docs.title: Using These Scripts
docs.text:
Scripts live in ~/scripts/ on any NeXuS node. The ncm/ subdirectory holds scripts specific to the connection manager.

# Run directly
~/scripts/ncm/nexus-ncm-certs.sh help

# Or add ~/scripts to PATH in your shell config
export PATH="$HOME/scripts:$HOME/scripts/ncm:$PATH"

All scripts respect these environment variables when set:

Variable Default Purpose NCM_CA_DIR ~/vault/ncm-ca mTLS certificate authority storage NCM_VPN_DIR ~/vault WireGuard and OpenVPN config files NEXUS_WEB_SERVER ~/Projects/nexus-web-server/nexus_web_server.py Web server path NEXUS_PROXY_SCRIPT ~/scripts/nexus-api-proxy.sh Proxy manager script

docs.title: nexus-ncm-certs.sh
docs.text:
mTLS client certificate manager for the NeXuS NCM web dashboard.

Location: ~/scripts/ncm/nexus-ncm-certs.sh Repo: hackenstacks/nexus-scripts · hackenstacks/nexus-connection-manager

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
The NCM web dashboard at https://localhost:8443/ncm/ includes a live terminal (xterm.js → PTY shell). mTLS locks it down so only browsers holding a valid client certificate can connect — rejection happens at the TLS handshake before any HTTP is served.

This script manages the full certificate lifecycle:

  • Creates a local CA (Certificate Authority) stored in ~/vault/ncm-ca/
  • Issues .p12 bundles (cert + key + CA, ready for browser import) for each trusted device
  • Revokes compromised certs and rebuilds the CRL
  • Patches the web server and proxy script to enforce client cert auth

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# 1. Create the CA (one time per node)
nexus-ncm-certs.sh init

# 2. Issue a cert for your laptop browser
nexus-ncm-certs.sh issue laptop
# → creates ~/vault/ncm-ca/clients/laptop.p12
# → prints a random import password

# 3. Wire the CA into the web server
nexus-ncm-certs.sh install

# 4. Restart the web server
nexus-api-proxy.sh restart

# 5. Import laptop.p12 into LibreWolf/Firefox:
#    Settings → Privacy & Security → Certificates → Your Certificates → Import

docs.title: init
docs.text:
Creates the Certificate Authority. Run once per node.

nexus-ncm-certs.sh init

Generates a 4096-bit RSA CA key and a self-signed CA certificate valid for 10 years. Both live in ~/vault/ncm-ca/ with permissions set to 700.

docs.title: issue <name>
docs.text:
Issues a client certificate for one trusted device.

nexus-ncm-certs.sh issue laptop
nexus-ncm-certs.sh issue phone
nexus-ncm-certs.sh issue anon-tablet

Each invocation:

  1. Generates a 2048-bit RSA key for the device
  2. Signs a certificate valid for 2 years
  3. Exports a .p12 bundle with a randomly-generated import password
  4. Prints the import password and browser import instructions

Keep the import password

The .p12 import password is printed once and saved alongside the file as <name>.pass. The password protects the key inside the .p12 — without it the browser cannot import the cert.

Transfer to another device:

# Via SCP
scp ~/vault/ncm-ca/clients/phone.p12 user@192.168.1.x:/tmp/

# As base64 (paste into remote terminal)
base64 ~/vault/ncm-ca/clients/phone.p12

Browser import:

Browser Path LibreWolf / Firefox Settings → Privacy & Security → Certificates → Your Certificates → Import Chromium / Chrome Settings → Privacy & Security → Manage Certificates → Import Android (Chrome) Settings → Security → Install a Certificate → VPN & App User Certificate

docs.title: list
docs.text:
Shows all issued certificates and their status.

nexus-ncm-certs.sh list

Output:

── NeXuS NCM Client Certificates ──

  CA: /home/user/vault/ncm-ca/ca.crt  (expires Sep  3 06:39:30 2036 GMT)

  NAME                  EXPIRES                       STATUS
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  laptop                Sep  3 06:39:30 2028 GMT       VALID
  phone                 Sep  3 06:39:30 2028 GMT       VALID
  old-device            Sep  3 06:39:30 2027 GMT       REVOKED

docs.title: revoke <name>
docs.text:
Revokes a certificate and rebuilds the CRL (Certificate Revocation List).

nexus-ncm-certs.sh revoke old-device
  • Marks the cert as revoked in the OpenSSL index
  • Rebuilds ~/vault/ncm-ca/crl.pem
  • Removes the .p12 so it cannot be re-imported
  • The revoked cert is rejected on the next TLS handshake after the web server reloads the CRL

Note

Restart the web server after revoking to enforce the new CRL immediately.

docs.title: install
docs.text:
Patches the web server to require client certificates on every connection.

nexus-ncm-certs.sh install

Two files are patched:

  1. nexus_web_server.py — adds --ca-cert and --ca-crl CLI arguments; wires them into the SSL context with ssl.CERT_REQUIRED
  2. nexus-api-proxy.sh — passes --ca-cert ~/vault/ncm-ca/ca.crt --ca-crl ~/vault/ncm-ca/crl.pem to the server start command

After running install, restart the web server. Any browser without a valid client cert will receive a TLS handshake failure — no HTTP response, no page, no error message to fingerprint.

docs.title: uninstall
docs.text:
Removes the client cert requirement (interactive confirmation required).

nexus-ncm-certs.sh uninstall

Removes the --ca-cert flags from nexus-api-proxy.sh. The web server reverts to HTTPS-only (no client cert check) after restart.

docs.title: show-ca
docs.text:
Prints the CA certificate in PEM format for importing into device trust stores.

nexus-ncm-certs.sh show-ca

Useful when a device needs to trust the CA (e.g., to avoid TLS warnings when accessing other services signed by the same CA).

docs.title: File Layout
docs.text:
~/vault/ncm-ca/
├── ca.key          — CA private key (600 permissions)
├── ca.crt          — CA certificate (import this on devices that need to trust the CA)
├── ca.srl          — Serial number counter
├── crl.pem         — Certificate Revocation List (rebuilt on every revoke)
├── index.txt       — OpenSSL certificate database
├── openssl.cnf     — OpenSSL CA configuration (auto-generated)
└── clients/
    ├── laptop.key  — Device private key (600)
    ├── laptop.crt  — Device certificate
    ├── laptop.p12  — Browser import bundle (cert + key + CA)
    └── laptop.pass — Import password (keep safe)

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text:
Browser (laptop.p12 installed)
    │
    │ TLS ClientHello + Certificate
    ▼
NeXuS Web Server (ssl.CERT_REQUIRED)
    │ Verifies against CA + CRL
    ├── VALID   → connection proceeds, HTTP served
    └── INVALID → TLS handshake fails, connection dropped
                  no HTTP response, no fingerprint

The CA key never leaves ~/vault/ncm-ca/. Client keys never leave the device they were issued for (the .p12 is the transfer mechanism — once imported and the file deleted from the target device, the key is only in the browser's certificate store).

docs.text: Variable Default Description NCM_CA_DIR ~/vault/ncm-ca CA and client cert storage NEXUS_PROXY_SCRIPT ~/scripts/nexus-api-proxy.sh Script to patch for mTLS NEXUS_WEB_SERVER ~/Projects/nexus-web-server/nexus_web_server.py Server to patch
